articles.title_orig: The US needs its own grey-zone tactics in the South China Sea - The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.title_zh: The US needs its own grey-zone tactics in the South China Sea - The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.source: The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.content_orig:
Passive resistance to Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea is not working. If the United States wants to win in the region, it needs a grey-zone strategy of its own.
Beijing has spent a decade refining a playbook that stays deliberately below the threshold of armed conflict. Chinese coast guard ships ram Philippine vessels, maritime militia swarm disputed reefs, and drones shadow foreign ships. Washington’s response – patrols, joint statements and expressions of concern – has imposed few costs and changed little.
This passivity means that China isn’t being deterred. Indeed, it’s being reassured that it can keep getting away with what it’s doing.
The US doesn’t need ships built for ramming to change that calculation. Rather, it should play to its strengths: a vast intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance network, powerful cyber and electromagnetic warfare capabilities and a web of regional partners. The US military’s F3EAD targeting cycle (find, fix, finish, exploit, analyse and disseminate) offers a template for response. For grey-zone competition, it can be adapted into F2RED: find, fix, respond, exploit and disseminate, with calibrated non-kinetic responses replacing the kinetic component (the ‘finish’).
The first two steps of the cycle that could be applied to the South China Sea are largely in place. Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets across the region already track Chinese coast guard, navy, and maritime militia vessels, and coordination with partner forces can expand the network even further. But after that there’s a gap, because of Washington’s reticence to respond with any operation that may cause escalation.
One response below the threshold of armed conflict is to apply soft-kill effects – that is, nothing with kinetic impact, at least not on anything very costly or with people in it. When Chinese vessels launch uncrewed aircraft to harass or surveil ships of US partners, allied forces can jam or bring down the drones on the spot. Operations can be conducted against Chinese drones elsewhere to divert Beijing’s attention from the area of tension. The same tools become more potent against larger, more expensive ships and aircraft. Crucially, these effects must be paired with signalling, making it clear to Beijing that if its vessels don’t break contact with partners, costs will follow.
Cyber is a second channel for imposing costs. Beyond highlighting Chinese cyber actions against the US and its partners, the US can integrate offensive cyber capabilities into the ‘respond’ phase. By imposing proportionate costs on Chinese government, military or coast guard entities or networks, the US can signal that continued Chinese grey-zone actions will have consequences. For example, if a Chinese vessel rams a Philippine ship, the US could respond by disrupting critical systems associated with Chinese maritime operations. Because such capabilities can be employed from outside the immediate area of a dispute, they also provide strategic depth and another means of responding to Chinese coercion.
The US Coast Guard and Navy can work alongside partner coast guards to block, stop, and arrest militia or fishing crews caught operating illegally in partner waters. The principle is simple: partners enforce their own laws in their own waters, with US ships and intelligence backing them. This must stay strictly legal and be confined to those breaking international law and the law of US partners. Done properly, it turns Beijing’s favoured tactic, coercion dressed as law enforcement, back on itself, but from firmer legal ground.
Financial tools should be tied to response options. In 2022, the US Treasury sanctioned Chinese distant-water fishing companies , adding more than 150 vessels to the Specially Designated Nationals list over human rights abuses and illegal fishing. Extending that precedent to illegal fishing and militia activity within the region would mean freezing assets and persuading banks to cut their ties, further complicating militia and fishing operations and imposing additional costs.
The last two steps in the chain – exploiting and disseminating – are where the US holds its greatest advantage. It already operates extensively with regional partners, so the infrastructure for sharing information exists. It simply needs to be expanded to countries bullied by China.
That should include tracking data. If China can ram Philippine ships in Philippine waters, Manila should receive the information it needs to enforce its own rights, lawfully, in waters that Beijing claims. That should involve all of the aforementioned strategies supported by US capabilities – enforcing exclusive economic zones by arresting illegal fishing vessels, partnering with the US to jam Chinese drones within those areas, or using US intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance networks to identify and remove Chinese intelligence and surveillance sensors within partners’ territories.
A US–China hotline could accompany all of this, alerting Beijing before the response phase commences and giving it a chance to back down.
Critics will warn that all this would risk escalation, and in the short term some friction would be likely. But Beijing currently pays nothing for testing its neighbours, and it will keep testing them until it pays much more. Demonstrating resolve, rather than tacitly accepting Chinese sovereignty claims, is more likely to lead to de-escalation over time.
Additionally, many regional states dislike China’s bullying but lack the resources to resist it alone. Seeing Washington finally impose costs, lawfully and alongside partners, could stiffen the resolve of those fence-sitters. In grey-zone competition, passivity is a strategy that’s working in Beijing’s favour.
William ‘Billy’ Price is a Major in the United States Marine Corps Reserve, has deployed to the Middle East and Africa as an intelligence officer, and has a master’s in International Service from American University.

articles.title_orig: US immigration authorities raid Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
articles.title_zh: US immigration authorities raid Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
articles.content_orig:
Watch: Agents seen outside US Congresswoman llhan Omar's home
US immigration agents searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a "criminal investigation".
Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorised search warrant" for the home in the Washington, DC area, a US justice department spokesperson told the BBC.
The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation," the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at the home.
Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponise federal law enforcement".
HSI agents loading a box outside the residence
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."
Her communications director Jacklyn Rogers called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration. "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."
The nature of the criminal investigation remains unclear.
A BBC crew saw several agents at the home, some carrying boxes to a van. News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which has said the investigation is about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.
The timing of Monday's raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - has raised concerns from Democrats who have rallied behind Omar.
The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or disadvantage a candidate.
The US House Democratic Party leadership said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump.
"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," it said.
Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow Congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena of her records.
Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar.
Separately, the White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.
Omar denied these allegations last month. "I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email, an archive of which has been seen by the BBC.
She has been targeted by Trump with the president previously suggesting that she "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House Representative.
Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession".
The president has also spoken unfavourably about the Somali American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back."
Some Republicans celebrated the search. "Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota Representative Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"
Omar is the first Somali-American elected to the US House of Representatives and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan Representative Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.
She won the 2024 election with 74% of the vote.
Senior political leaders in Minnesota have also criticised the search. Governor Tim Walz criticised the search on Monday. "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."
Minnesota senator Tina Smith called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections."
Additional reporting by Ione Wells

articles.title_orig: Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ collides with real-world problems of dwindling fuel supplies
articles.title_zh: Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ collides with real-world problems of dwindling fuel supplies
articles.content_orig:
US President Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that an energy ceasefire had been reached between Ukraine and Russia that was "effective immediately".
Ukraine's President Zelensky responded by saying his country is willing to back an energy ceasefire if Russia does the same, adding it could "become a major step toward ending the war".
However, Moscow hasn't confirmed its agreement and Zelensky said Russia hit a Ukrainian power plant in Kharkiv "immediately after" Trump's post over the weekend.
The BBC's Ukraine correspondent Dan Johnson reports from Kyiv, where Ukrainians are facing another winter with electricity outages that leave people without heat, light or even water.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskyy says Russia strikes energy facilities despite Trump claim of an energy ceasefire
articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy says Russia strikes energy facilities despite Trump claim of an energy ceasefire
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday that Russia has continued to strike Ukraine's energy facilities even after U.S. President Donald Trump said a day earlier that the warring countries had agreed on an energy ceasefire in the 4 1/2-year-old war.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learned through media reports that Trump had secured an energy ceasefire deal with Russia which would involve a mutual pause in strikes on energy sites. Zelenskyy said he would be willing to honor such an agreement, if Moscow did the same.
“We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump’s brief social media post on Sunday claiming the purported agreement offered few details but said that the energy ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!”
Yet Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been “horribly surprised" that following Trump's "sudden but very important post,” Russia had struck numerous energy facilities including a power plant in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, as well as a gas production facility and a civilian gas station.
“It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said, referring to Trump's social media platform.
Energy strikes have caused pain for both Ukraine and Russia
Trump previously announced a similar agreement on ceasing energy strikes that did not come to fruition. In a social media post on Sept. 14, he said both countries had agreed “not to hit” each other’s energy infrastructure, but offered no details on that proposal either.
Russia has used attacks on energy facilities in order to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as “weaponizing winter," and fear Russia could ramp up such attacks as cold weather approaches.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has launched strikes against Russian energy sites like oil refineries, sometimes deep within Russian territory, prompting Trump to blame Zelenskyy for high diesel prices on world markets. On Friday, Trump struck a deal with Putin to import Russian diesel in an attempt to address high fuel prices just weeks ahead of U.S. midterm elections.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to comply with Trump's requests to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, and asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree. He added that if Moscow does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, “we will respond.”
“We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said. “This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war.”
EU foreign policy chief skeptical of energy ceasefire
The European Union’s top diplomat on Monday welcomed the prospect of a pause in energy strikes in Ukraine, but said she sees no sign that Russia would be willing to respect it.
“We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said at a meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers in Luxembourg. “Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy.”
Trump's deal with Putin to purchase diesel from Russia dismayed officials in the U.S., Ukraine and around Europe. A bipartisan group of six senators, including four Republicans, called on the Trump administration on Sunday to “immediately reverse course” on the deal, saying the U.S. should “not provide Putin with a financial lifeline” while Russia is killing Ukrainian civilians.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told reporters in Luxembourg on Monday that he doesn’t believe the deal would meaningfully affect fuel prices, and that it is ”much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S."
Kallas also pushed back on Trump's comments on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to get a new president and that Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war. She said that now is not the time to hold elections in Ukraine, at least not without a ceasefire.
On Monday, Zelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine was impossible during war time, especially with new Russian tactics involving attacks during both the day and night. He added, however, that he would be ready to work towards doing so if Ukraine secured a full ceasefire lasting at least 60 days.
Russian attack kills 3 and injures others, including children
Two people were injured in Russian daytime strikes on Kyiv on Monday, according to the city's military administration, while falling debris from Russian attacks sparked a fire in a private residential building in the capital's Darnytskyi district.
Debris also fell in an open area near private residential buildings in the Solomianskyi district, and on a warehouse building in the Darnytskyi district, with emergency services dispatched to the scene.
A Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor’s Office. Investigators said the attack struck a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores and sparking a fire.
Ukrainian air defense forces shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones overnight Monday, Ukraine’s Air Force said in a Telegram post. The attack involved one Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and 121 drones, including 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, the statement said.
Strikes were recorded at 15 locations in Ukraine, while debris from downed drones fell at four locations.
The Russian Defense Ministry on Monday said its air defenses overnight intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions as well as the illegally annexed Crimea and the waters of the Black Sea.
In a separate statement, the ministry said its forces overnight carried out drone strikes on Ukraine’s unspecified port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Ukraine's port city of Odesa with military cargo on board.
Associated Press writer Lorne Cook in Brussels contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: British adventurer returns home after 28-year walk around the world
articles.title_zh: British adventurer returns home after 28-year walk around the world
articles.content_orig:
Adventurer Karl Bushby has finally stepped foot on UK soil as he completes a 28-year long journey across the world, Fox News' Stephanie Bennett reports.
Adventurer Karl Bushby has finally stepped foot on UK soil after a 28-year journey across the world.
On Oct. 5, he announced he swam the English Channel , from France to England. While resting in Dover, he said, "I’m staring at the Union Jack flying outside this hotel. I’ve seen many flags over the days, but that one is special."
On social media he shared one of his first meals back, overjoyed to have authentic British fish and chips again.
DALE 'GREY BEARD' SANDERS RECLAIMS TITLE AS OLDEST PERSON TO THRU-HIKE THE APPALACHIAN TRAIL AT 91
Karl Bushby celebrates after swimming across the Caspian Sea from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan in September 2024. (Resul Rehimov/Anadolu via Getty Images)
His journey is not over yet. He hopes to reach the finish line — his mother’s home in Hull — by the end of the month.
According to his website , he received a birthday card in the 1990s from his father about two soldiers arguing over an impossible feat, walking from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Karl grabbed a map and drew a single line, knowing he found his life’s mission.
NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11
Bushby is shown moving through Dover, England, on Oct. 9 as he begins the final 250-mile leg of his 28-year journey.
On Nov. 1, 1998, the ex-paratrooper started his journey in Chile, with only a few hundred dollars in his pocket "South America, you were young, it was all new, it was the boys adventure dream," Bushby said.
He walked north to the United States, waiting for the Bering Strait to freeze to cross from Alaska into Russia. In April 2012, Russia denied his next visa, pausing his expedition. So he started walking in the wrong direction, in protest, to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C. The ban was overturned and he carried on with his journey. From Russia he entered Mongolia, China, and swam the Caspian Sea from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan.
"You’ll find that you are way more capable than you think you are, people always underestimate themselves. The world always looks bigger and scarier than it actually is," Bushby said.
MAN WHO BEAT RARE CANCER CELEBRATES BY CANOEING 2,000 MILES WITH HIS DOG
Bushby walked through Cameron, North Carolina, in 2014 during the U.S. leg of his journey. (Megan Morr/Washington Post)
He originally expected the journey to take 12 years, but visa restrictions, the 2008 financial crash, COVID-19 , geopolitics, detention and some close calls slowed his progress. He says it’s the people that kept him going.
"The world is an incredible place, and it’s the people, the strangers that I have met along the way, that have kept me upright and moving forward," Bushby said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Bushby has roughly 240 miles left to walk. He covered more than 30,000 miles, across 29 countries. "We went at a reasonable pace, we did what we needed to do and it has worked. I know it’s time to stop, I know that much because I feel that in the knees and ankles."
Stephanie Bennett currently serves as a London-based reporter for Fox News Channel (FNC).

articles.title_orig: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included pregnant daughter of gunman
articles.title_zh: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included pregnant daughter of gunman
articles.content_orig:
The victims of a mass shooting in northwest Pennsylvania included the gunman’s wife and pregnant daughter who was due to give birth on Monday, authorities said.
Matthew Stone , 45, died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound on Friday after killing six members of his own family and two neighbors, Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook told NBC News on Monday.
Victims included the shooter’s wife Michelle Stone, 44, pregnant daughter Angelina K. Stone, 24, and sons Matthew Stone Jr. 21, and  Jonathan Stone, 19, according to the coroner.
Angelina Stone was carrying “an unborn fetus who was supposed to have been born today,” Cook said.
Two other unidentified children, a 5-year-old boy and a nearly 2-year-old girl, were also related the shooter and killed inside the house, according to the coroner.
All of the Stones lived at that Perry Street home while victims Twila A. Tanner, 51, and Lora Lee Roberts, 37, were neighbors who were fatally shot outside, Cook said.
Juicesiyah Alexander Ezekiel , father of the slain little girl, said he’s struggling to understand why the elder Stone opened fire.
“I wouldn’t even put this on my worst enemy man,” Ezekiel told NBC affiliate WICU. “It’s sickening.”
The little girl was going to turn 2 next month.
“Her name is Amari’anna,” Ezekiel said. “She’s the most beautiful baby God could have created.”
Senior Breaking News Reporter

articles.title_zh: Meta releases its first frontier model, Muse Wonder
articles.content_orig:
Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.
Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card ), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.
That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API. Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.
In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”
To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark , which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.
“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.
The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year . Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio , which came online earlier this year.

articles.title_orig: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.title_zh: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.content_orig:
A federal judge expressed alarm at how quickly the Trump administration moved to use taxpayer funds for midterm election advertisements following an Oval Office meeting between President Donald Trump and Republican operatives.
U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon issued a temporary restraining order Sunday to immediately stop the propaganda ads, a win for pro-democracy groups who argue they are an illegal misuse of funds appropriated by Congress.
The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) was able to shift $20 million for the ads in a matter of hours, Rochon said in a 40-page opinion Monday explaining her decision.  The restraining order is necessary to ensure the government doesn’t just “reapportion funds from another source to continue running similar advertisements,” she wrote.
The New York Times reported earlier this month that Trump and his White House chief of staff, Susie Wiles, met with Republican strategists on August 7 to talk about the midterms and how to use money from a super PAC to support Republican candidates.
“During that meeting, President Trump reportedly expressed a desire to promote his administration and showed the strategists videos of himself, including footage later incorporated into one of the challenged advertisements,” Rochon wrote in her opinion.
Trump then tapped OMB Director Russell Vought to “find government funds to pay for the advertisements,” she added.
“Defendants do not deny that this meeting took place or dispute the reported substance of the various discussions, even though the Court expressly asked Defendants during the [temporary restraining order] conference on October 9, 2026 to address whether they disputed the reports of this meeting,” Rochon wrote.
Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.
Little over a month after the Oval Office meeting, the funds were made available through a U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) account for “commemorative events.” The process took just a few hours, the judge said.
“OMB initially apportioned $500,000 towards the commemorative category in November 2025,” Rochon wrote in her opinion. “On September 19, 2026, at 6:15 p.m., CBP submitted a request to OMB to reapportion funds that were appropriated by section 90004 of the Working Families Tax Cut Act within CBP’s ‘Operations and Support’ account. The CBP request sought to make an additional $20 million available for obligations under line 6043 for ‘commemorative events’ by reallocating funds from the following fiscal year. The request was approved by OMB that evening, less [than] two hours later, at 7:50 p.m.”
The next day, on Sept. 20, CBP made a $20 million purchase to LMD Agency for a “National Media Campaign.”
“The present apportionment was done quickly … and President Trump has publicly conveyed his belief that using appropriated taxpayer money is not only legal but a ‘standard thing to do,’” Rochon wrote.
In addition to not receiving “reasonable assurances” that the White House won’t find funds from another source to keep running the same or similar ads, Rochon said it’s unclear where the initial media buy stands.
A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official told the court that the department hadn’t directed LMD to make “any additional” ad purchases past October 11.
“But this representation is somewhat unclear and leaves open whether LMD has already purchased ad placements scheduled to air after October 11, thereby continuing the alleged harm” to pro-democracy groups, Rochon said.
“Even if LMD has not purchased any further media buys for placement after October 11, Defendants have not shown that the ‘allegedly wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur,’” Rochon wrote.
The judge ordered the Trump administration to report back on its compliance with her order within 24 hours. Under the temporary restraining order , DHS can’t create, disseminate or air the challenged advertisements or enter into new contracts to do so.

articles.title_orig: Micron stock drops on China CXMT denser memory chip news
articles.title_zh: Micron stock drops on China CXMT denser memory chip news
articles.content_orig:
ChangXin Memory Technologies plans to release a server memory chip with a 4F square design by year-end, rattling memory stocks globally
Micron $MU Technology stock fell Monday after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies announced progress on a new chip design that can pack more data onto a single chip. Micron stock was down about 3% to $998.15 in Monday trading, putting it on track for a third consecutive losing session.
According to the South China Morning Post , which cited a company statement, CXMT President Cao Kanyu told attendees at a Shanghai industry event over the weekend that the company intends to launch a new server memory product before the end of 2026. The so-called 4F square design places each memory cell within an area equal to four times the square of F — the minimum line width of a semiconductor — enabling a greater number of cells to fit on the same chip.
The announcement rippled through the broader memory sector. Shares of SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, both of which have been exploring the same 4F square architecture, also declined. SK Hynix American depositary receipts shed roughly 3.6%, and Samsung Electronics finished the session down 4.4%. Sandisk tumbled 5.7%, with hard disk-drive manufacturers Seagate $STX and Western Digital $WDC posting losses of 3.4% and 2.3%.
Investors have monitored CXMT as a potential disruptor to the memory market. When CXMT made its trading debut in July, its shares rocketed 466%, lifting the company's market capitalization to just under $500 billion, according to Barron's . As of Monday’s close, CXMT remained China’s largest company by total valuation, ahead of Tencent and state-owned banks China Construction Bank and Agricultural Bank of China, according to Barron’s.
Micron stock had been among the strongest performers in the market this year heading into Monday. Memory chip makers have benefited from surging demand tied to AI data center construction, which has kept supply tight and driven up prices for high-capacity memory. Micron stock was up 261% for the year through Friday's close.
Analyst Jim Cramer argued in August that memory manufacturers had changed their behavior by locking in revenue through extended customer contracts rather than expanding production to chase volume — a shift he said made the sector's rally more durable than past cycles. He flagged a surge in new manufacturing capacity, including from Samsung, as among the key risks that could end the rally.

articles.title_orig: Now 50 Years Old, One of the World’s Most Diverse Collection of Organisms Lives On at UT
articles.title_zh: Now 50 Years Old, One of the World’s Most Diverse Collection of Organisms Lives On at UT
articles.content_orig:
David Nobles Jr., curator of the UTEX Culture Collection of Algae, looks back and explains why algae matter in research.
UTEX distributes thousands of algae cultures like these to researchers, educators and companies in every state in the U.S. and dozens of countries around the world every year. Photo credit: Eileen Chong
In 2026, a remarkable collection, unique to The University of Texas in Austin, celebrated its 50th anniversary –– the UTEX Culture Collection of Algae. David Nobles Jr., just the third curator of the collection in its 50 years, is charged with maintaining one of the most diverse collections of organisms anywhere on Earth.
Nobles is a world-class phycologist, the term he and his colleagues prefer for a person who studies algae (the other term, “algologist , ” also applies to people who study pain, and Nobles quipped that, though there can be days when that feels fitting, a distinction should be made). This summer, he and his colleagues moved their entire collection, more than 1,500 species, into a new space in the Moffett Molecular Biology Building at UT. We spoke with him to learn about the importance of the collection. This conversation has been edited for space.
David Nobles crouching amidst hundreds of vials containing algae strains housed in the UTEX Culture Collection of Algae. Photo credit: Eileen Chong
Why is algae so important to catalog and understand, and do you have an example from your own research?
Algae have been found to have tremendous commercial applications, from pharmaceuticals to fuel to mining. For example, phosphate is a limited resource vital to all agriculture, and algae are used to recover it from wastewater. Last year, we got a grant with a group from Sandia National Laboratories in Los Alamos to study algae that bind to rare earth elements. There are few accessible sources of such elements, which is why we call them rare, but these are critical minerals for our modern electronics, computers and phones. Some algae not only bind to these minerals naturally and efficiently, they can be made to collect the precious minerals in wastewater. So, we’ve been studying, including with an incredible group of undergraduates, which algae to use for bio-mining. It’s pretty amazing. Algae may give us an environmentally friendly way to mine rare earth metals.
What’s more, more than half of all carbon dioxide that’s naturally removed from our atmosphere is done so by algae. Algae are vital to our planet’s health. These organisms are also the bottom of the food chain in the oceans. Without them, there would be no marine life. They are often used to feed farm animals, so they are a primary source of protein and nutrients for us, too (plus, pretty much any time you buy a green smoothie to be healthy, one of its main ingredients is spirulina, a kind of algae). Of course, algae also frequently disrupt our lives, such as the frequent cyanobacterial blooms in lakes when no one can swim. For all these reasons, understanding algae better is critical.
One of Noble’s favorite algae in UTEX is Valonia ventricosa (UTEX 2260), which forms bubbles of air surrounded by protoplasm. The original sample of this specimen was collected in 1970 from Coconut Island in Kaneohe Bay off the island of Oahu, Hawaii, and deposited into the collection in 1975, just a year before the move to UT.
Maybe I should also ask: What is algae?
Well, I like to tell people that algae is plural. That’s a good place to start because there is no singular group of organisms we can call alga.
Have you ever seen the tree of life? There are a few big domains like the eukaryotes, bacteria and archaea. Humans are on a single branch, near the bottom with all the other animals, under the eukaryotes. Plants are in another group of eukaryotes nearby. That means, even the most amazing zoo in the world focuses on organisms from only one group, the animals. The lushest botanical garden anywhere focuses on organisms from only one group, the plants. But what we call algae are not a single natural group. They are on many branches. So, we have 3,000 organisms from across the tree of life that we call algae. That’s why I always say our collection is perhaps the most diverse collection of living organisms in the world.
What we call algae are different organisms that share one characteristic. Most are a single cell, but they all use chlorophyll-a to gather energy from the sun through photosynthesis. And though they are green, they can be distinguished from plants because algae don’t have structures like roots, stems and leaves. Even so, plants stem from one group of algae in the tree of life, so one of my colleagues jokingly refers to plants as “higher and drier algae.” I like that.
David Nobles holds up an Erlenmeyer flask containing red algae called Gracilaria verrucosa (UTEX 2206). This particular strain is used to make agar, a growth medium used widely in microbiology. The algae in the flask are descended from a sample collected in 1973 from Port Aransas Bay, Texas, and deposited in UTEX in 1979. Photo credit: Eileen Chong
How did the UTEX collection start?
Richard Starr, the founder of our collection, met a man named Ernst Pringsheim in 1953, who gifted him some cultures when they were both at Cambridge University in England. Pringsheim was one of the first people to study and grow algae in the early 1900s, and he escaped from the Nazis with his collection of about 400 strains several years before meeting Starr. Starr brought cultures back to the United States and grew the cultures into a collection, eventually returning to where he had gotten his Ph.D., here at UT. When he returned in 1976, he brought 2,000 strains with him, taking over a space in the Biological Laboratories Building and renamed it the UTEX Culture Collection. He was the director until he passed away unexpectedly in 1998, when Jerry Brand succeeded him. The collection still exists today largely because of Brand’s dedication and skill. We still have some of the original strains from the early 1900s in the collection because of him. Jerry retired in 2015, and I became just the third director. This year, the collection’s 50th anniversary, we finally moved out of our old space and into a new one in the Moffett Molecular Biology Building, a more modern space for the collection.
How did the collection grow to what it is today?
Mostly, the collection grew by accretion. Many researchers have private collections. After they retire, they will bequeath us their most important organisms, to take care of and make available to others. It’s a big responsibility, taking care of someone else’s life’s work. But it’s also a tremendous honor to do this for the community. I’ve just done my best to be a good steward of the collection.
Do you have any famous strains of algae in the collection?
We have the algae used in the original experiments that revealed the Calvin cycle. That’s the process in which carbon is removed from the air by photosynthetic organisms to make sugars, which not only helps the organisms grow but also provides food for all living creatures on Earth. Most people learn about it in school.
Algae in the genus Acetabularia , another of Noble’s favorites, are sometimes called maiden’s or mermaid’s wineglass because of their shape. These algae are notable for being unicellular, despite reaching lengths of 7-8 centimeters (about 3 inches). This specimen is Acetabularia farlowii (UTEX 2701), which was originally collected from Padre Island, Texas in 1975 and deposited into UTEX in 1976.
What’s a normal day like with the collection?
It’s a very hands-on job, taking care of 3,000 strains of living organisms. Jerry Brand, our former director, grew up on a farm, and he said the work was basically the same: Cows have to be milked every day; algae have to be tended to. That means we don’t get much time off. Most of our work is making food, what we call media, to grow the cultures. Algae can be pretty picky about what they consu

articles.title_orig: Apple 'Welcome Home' Launch: Everything to Expect Tomorrow
articles.title_zh: Apple 'Welcome Home' Launch: Everything to Expect Tomorrow
articles.content_orig:
Apple's "Welcome Home" product launch is happening tomorrow. As the name suggests, Apple is going to debut new home accessories, including the long-rumored home hub.
Below, we've listed all the rumors we know about the three devices Apple is set to introduce.
Apple's home hub, which will be called HomeView , is a multi-function device designed for all of a home's occupants. It's built around Siri AI, and will have an A18 chip and 8GB of RAM.
Here's what rumors suggest it'll be able to do:
The hub will be able to do anything you might want a home assistant device to do, from giving the next steps of a recipe to suggesting dinner ideas and creating a shopping list. It will rely heavily on ‌Siri‌ AI for voice-based input, but it will also have a 6-inch touch display.
The display is square with bezels around the edges, and there are two models. One version can be mounted on the wall, and the other is attached to a half-dome speaker base with a flexible arm for adjusting tilt. The hub isn't expected to have its own App Store , but it will support Apple apps such as Safari, News, Music, Reminders, Calendar, Weather, Messages, FaceTime , Photos , and Mail.
There will be a presence sensor and a camera in the hub, and it will use a variation of Face ID to determine who is nearby to show customized content. It will display information from a linked iPhone, like email messages, but only after authenticating. The sensors in the hub will be usable in HomeKit scenes and automations, so you can use it to trigger lights and other devices when a person walks into the room.
The interface will be heavily widget-based so you can see information at a glance, and it's likely going to look similar to StandBy mode on the iPhone. You will be able to choose your preferred clock face or idle state, along with a home screen of widget options that you can tap to open a full app. If you have multiple hubs, they'll link together for features like multi-room music and intercom functionality. Rumors suggest that it will have better sound quality than the HomePod mini .
There isn't going to be a built-in battery, and the hub will need to be connected to power via an included USB-C port. The speaker-equipped version is expected in multiple colors, including gray, silver, starlight, and rose. The wall-mounted version will be available in silver and gray.
Rumors suggest the hub could be priced somewhere around $350.
Apple isn't updating the design of the Apple TV , so expect the new model to be the same boring black box. What's changing is entirely inside.
The ‌Apple TV‌ 4K is going to get a lot more powerful so it can support ‌Siri‌ AI, offering many of the same ‌Siri‌ features that are available on iPhone and iPad in iOS and iPadOS 27 .
We're expecting an A19 with 8GB of RAM, along with Apple's N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Thread. The A19 will bring a major upgrade in performance, both for ‌Siri‌ and for gaming. It has ray tracing, mesh shading, and other features that will improve gameplay graphics.
There will be a new ‌Siri‌ Remote with an included speaker to make it easier to find, and we've seen some signs that Apple is working on its own gaming controller under the Beats brand , but there's no word on whether it's ready to launch.
Apple will likely emphasize ‌Siri‌ AI and gaming capabilities when introducing the ‌Apple TV‌. Apple raised the price of the current ‌Apple TV‌ to $199 in June, and the new model will be at least that expensive with the processor and RAM upgrades.
Like the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K, the ‌HomePod mini‌ isn't going to get a new design, but it will have internal upgrades that make it more capable. It's going to get an upgraded S10 chip, second-generation UWB for features like Handoff, and the N1 networking chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
You'll need a nearby AI-capable device for ‌Siri‌ AI processing because the HomePod probably won't be able to handle much on-device, but smarter ‌Siri‌ should make for a better experience. ‌Siri‌ AI on ‌HomePod mini‌ will have the context of ‌Siri‌ interactions on other devices, and it's likely conversations will be saved to a connected iPhone's ‌Siri‌ app.
‌Siri‌ AI can answer follow-up questions, handle multi-request queries, and access information from your apps. It'll be similar to having ChatGPT or Claude on a speaker. Though design updates aren't expected, the ‌HomePod mini‌ will get new colors. We're expecting white, blue, black, sage, and pink.
‌HomePod mini‌ pricing went up from $99 to $129 in June 2026, and the new model will likely be priced at $129 too.
Apple worked with LG to make an LG-branded wired video doorbell, thermostat, smart deadbolt lock, temperature sensor, indoor security camera, outdoor security camera, and floodlight camera that will work with the home hub and the ‌HomeKit‌ platform.
The accessories are part of an "Apple Home Collection" that will be marketed alongside the HomeView. They won't be ready until later this year at the earliest, but Apple could show them off during the announcement.
There's no keynote event for the "Welcome Home" product debut, so Apple is probably going to release a video and an accompanying set of press releases. There's an NYC media event that's going to take place at 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday, October 13, and that could be when all of the announcements happen.
The NYC event will let members of the media get some hands-on time with the new devices to share first impressions.
Apple could begin accepting pre-orders just after the new devices launch. The ‌HomePod mini‌ and the ‌Apple TV‌ 4K are going to launch on Friday, October 30.
The HomeView won't be available right away and is expected to ship to customers in mid-November .

articles.title_orig: Sixth person who had measles has died in Pennsylvania, local coroner says
articles.title_zh: Sixth person who had measles has died in Pennsylvania, local coroner says
articles.content_orig:
The death of a 39-year-old Franklin County woman has marked Pennsylvania’s sixth measles-associated death in 2026, according to county officials.
The Franklin County Coroner’s Office said it investigated the woman’s death Saturday. She had several underlying health conditions, including a recent measles diagnosis for which she received treatment.
According to the coroner’s office, the case meets the Pennsylvania Department of Health’s definition of a "measles-associated death." It is the first such death reported in Franklin County in many years.
The state Department of Health defines a confirmed measles-associated death as one occurring within 30 days of symptom onset in a person who had clinical evidence of measles, a positive laboratory test and no unrelated cause of death. The classification does not necessarily mean measles was the sole cause of death.
The coroner’s office said it would not release additional information that could identify the woman, citing privacy laws and respect for her family.
"Our office is bound by laws that limit what can be shared publicly, and families deserve the dignity to mourn in private," the office said in a statement.
County officials urged health care professionals, first responders and residents to follow guidance from the Pennsylvania Department of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
"Caution and vigilance are key to our success in the treatment of this disease and its aftereffects," the coroner's office said.
The Department of Health says measles is highly contagious and spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. State health officials say vaccination provides the best protection against the disease.

General Onsale Begins on Friday, October 16 at 10am local time on LiveNation.com
2X GRAMMY®-nominated global Afrobeats superstar Ayra Starr announces the Starrgirl World Tour , a 20-city international run in support of her latest critically acclaimed new album, Starrgirl , released August 14.
The Starrgirl World Tour kicks off in Europe on January 20 at Live Music Hall in Cologne, Germany, and hits major cities including Amsterdam, Paris, Milan, Zurich, and Brussels before wrapping the leg in London on February 2. The tour then arrives in North America on March 18 at House of Blues in Houston, and hits cities including Atlanta, Brooklyn, Toronto, Chicago, and more, before wrapping on April 14 at The Fillmore in San Francisco. Before taking Starrgirl around the world in 2027, Ayra will close out this year with a special return to Africa. Further details will be announced soon.
Starrgirl notably debuted at No. 2 on Spotify’s Top Albums Global Chart, earning 3.9 million streams on Spotify in its first full day globally, and notably debuted at No. 1 on Apple Music’s album chart in 15 countries. Building on the album's momentum, Ayra Starr released the official video for “Heaven Baby” featuring ZAYN last week. “Heaven Baby,” quickly became a viral fan favorite track garnering over 43.2 million global streams, and reaching No. 1 on Shazam Global Viral chart within the first week of its release. Yesterday, Ayra made history as the first Afrobeats artist to headline an NFL International Game halftime show, taking the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London during the Philadelphia Eagles–Jacksonville Jaguars matchup.
Now with over 7 BILLION global streams, 1 BILLION YouTube views and a string of instantly-recognizable collaborations across different genres; it is clear Ayra Starr brings her culture with her wherever she goes – breaking barriers and creating ‘firsts’ for African artists.
Listen to Starrgirl HERE - out now via Mavin Recods/Republic Records.
TICKETS - NORTH AMERICA: Tickets will be available starting with a Verizon presale (details below) beginning on Tuesday, October 13 at 10 am local time and a Spotify Reserved presale beginning on Tuesday, October 13 at 2 pm local time. The artist presale begins Wednesday, October 14 at 10 am local time. Additional presales will run throughout the week ahead of the general onsale beginning on Friday, October 16 at 10am local time at Livenation.com.
TICKETS - EUROPE /UK: Tickets will be available starting an artist and Mastercard presale (details below) beginning on Wednesday, October 14 at 10 am local time. Additional presales will run throughout the week ahead of the general onsale beginning on Friday, October 16 at 10am local time at Livenation.com .
VIP: The tour will also offer a variety of different VIP packages and experiences for fans to take their concert experience to the next level. Packages vary but include premium tickets, post-show meet & greet and photo opportunity, autographed tour poster, early entry prior to public doors & more. VIP package contents vary based on the offer selected. For more information, visit vipnation.com!

Wed, Jan 20 – Cologne, DE – Live Music Hall Thurs, Jan 21 – Amsterdam, NL – Melkweg Sun, Jan 24 – Paris, FR – Zenith Paris Wed, Jan 27 – Milan, IT – Fabrique Fri, Jan 29 – Zurich, CH – X-tra Sun, Jan 31 – Brussels, BE – Forest National Tue, Feb 2 – London, UK – Shepherd’s Bush Empire

2X GRAMMY®-nominated global Afrobeats superstar Ayra Starr has quickly become one of this generation’s most undeniable new voices in music. Renowned for her anthemic Afrobeats tracks and unapologetic style, the Beninese-Nigerian artist has amassed critical acclaim from tastemaker press, a massive international following, over 7 billion global streams, and 1 billion YouTube views. Following the release of her defining debut album 19 & Dangerous, her position as Africa’s hottest rising star has seen Ayra Starr tapped for collaborations with some of music’s biggest names, including Wizkid, Stormzy, Rema, Coldplay, and co-signs from the likes of Rihanna. The rising star gained major traction over the last few years but vaulted to the forefront of Afrobeats with 2022’s “Rush,” which gathered nearly 1 billion global streams and attracted R&B icon Kelly Rowland on a high-powered remix. Ayra notably picked up nominations at the Billboard Music Awards, BET Awards, MTV VMAs, and Soul Train Awards. She made history at the MOBO Awards as the first African woman to win Best International Act and the first woman in 16 years to win Best African Music Act. She earned her first GRAMMY® nomination for Best African Music Performance for “Rush,” cementing her as the first and youngest Nigerian female artist ever nominated in that category in 2024. Her momentum continued the next year with another GRAMMY® nomination for Best African Music Performance for her electrifying collaboration with Wizkid on “Gimme Dat.” Ayra continued to make waves with smash hits “Hot Body,” “Who’s Dat Girl,” and “Where Do We Go” which she performed on The Jennifer Hudson Show earlier this year. Now entering a bold new era, Ayra Starr released her highly anticipated album Starrgirl in August, featuring the hit single “Where Do We Go,” which was released earlier this year and has already amassed over 10 million streams. A genre-breaking, generation-defining talent, Ayra Starr continues to bring Afrobeats to the forefront here in the U.S. and across the world redefining what it means to be a global superstar.

articles.title_orig: Teen killed, 24 injured by unexploded Hezbollah munition on hike near Lebanon border
articles.title_zh: Teen killed, 24 injured by unexploded Hezbollah munition on hike near Lebanon border
articles.content_orig:
One teenager was killed and others were wounded, according to Israeli emergency response services, after an explosion on an Israeli school trip near the Lebanon border.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said an initial review by soldiers at the scene indicated that explosion was caused by an unexploded Hezbollah munition that had fallen in the area. It’s unclear when the projectile was fired. Pictures released by the IDF showed a military helicopter evacuating patients for medical treatment.
“Apparently, the suspicion is that an unexploded munition of some kind exploded in the hands of one of the students,” said Deputy Police Commissioner Meir Eliyahu, a commander in Israel’s northern district, according to Reuters.
According to United Hatzalah, an Israeli emergency response service, three people sustained serious injuries in the explosion, while at least 10 others suffered light-to-moderate injuries. The wounded were evacuated to three hospitals in the area, police said.
In a statement, the Ma’alot-Tarshiha municipality in northern Israel said students and staff were on the local school’s annual trip when the explosion happened. The country’s Ministry of Education said it was an “extremely difficult incident, and our thoughts are with the victims and their families.” Commissioner Daniel Levy told Reuters it was a “very serious incident, in which children who went on a field trip were hurt, to our sorrow.”
On Monday evening, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, along with Israel’s education minister, visited the wounded and their families at Rambam Hospital in Haifa. Netanyahu instructed the IDF to reinforce the prohibitions against touching unexploded ordinance.
Shortly after the explosion occurred on Monday afternoon, Israel Police said the initial suspicion was that the explosion was a result of an unexploded munition along the border near the villages of Yiftah and Manara. Bomb disposal experts were dispatched to examine the cause of the explosion, police said.
MDA said it was a “complex incident” as they sent numerous teams to the site. “We quickly dispatched substantial forces to the scene, including ambulances, mobile intensive care units (MICUs), and an MDA helicopter, which was also scrambled to the incident,” said regional director Itzik Shushan.
A US-brokered ceasefire in late-June was supposed to end months of conflict in southern Lebanon as it paved the way for the deployment of the Lebanese military and the gradual withdrawal of the IDF. Israel pulled back from two small areas along the so-called yellow line that demarcates the zone occupied by the Israeli military, but further progress on the agreement has largely stalled.
Israel has razed entire villages in southern Lebanon and has continued to carry out regular strikes there as it tries to remove Hezbollah from the territory.

Duckweed on end of pencil. (University of Nottingham via SWNS)
The world’s smallest flowering plant would be an “ideal” food crop for future space missions , according to new research.
Duckweeds measure just a few millimeters across, but scientists say they could feed astronauts exploring deep space — as well as providing a potential source of food and protein on Earth.
Researchers at the University of Nottingham conducted gene expression analysis and cutting-edge microscopy on duckweeds.
Their findings, published in the journal Current Biology , show that they retain the same basic building blocks found in the shoots of larger plants.
But those structures have been “dramatically compressed” and fused together.
(Photo by Samiran Biswas via Pexels)
Study leader Anthony Bishopp says miniaturization is a “remarkable phenomenon” found throughout the natural world, from tiny animals to miniature plants.
He said: “Duckweeds are extraordinary flowering plants that can measure just a few millimeters across, yet their relatives include some of the largest herbaceous plants.
“We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space.
“While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.
“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there.
“Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant.
(Photo by Petr Ganaj via Pexels)
“That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”
Bishopp said duckweed research is advancing rapidly, driven by growing interest in the tiny plants as a potential source of food and novel protein on Earth, as well as a possible crop for future space missions.
He added: “Unlike most of the crops we grow today, which have been shaped by thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, the potential of duckweed remains largely unexplored.
“Even the basic architecture of the duckweed plant has remained something of a mystery.
“Understanding how its body is organized provides an essential framework for understanding how duckweed grows, develops and functions — and ultimately how its potential might be improved.”
Study co-author Alex Ware said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case.”
Ware added: “Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”

articles.title_orig: US attorney warns Chinese espionage is 'extremely pervasive,' says Beijing 'playing the long game'
articles.title_zh: US attorney warns Chinese espionage is 'extremely pervasive,' says Beijing 'playing the long game'
articles.content_orig:
First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told Fox News Digital that Chinese government-backed espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said Chinese espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S. following the arrest of an alleged Chinese agent in Los Angeles this month.
Essayli told Fox News Digital in an interview that his office has pressed charges against several alleged Chinese spies in recent months, saying Beijing is brazen in its attempts to build their access inside the U.S.
"I think it's extremely pervasive," Essayli said of Chinese spying. " China is one of our biggest adversaries, and they're committed to advancing their interests. And they're playing the long game, and so they are willing to put a lot of resources into developing sources, recruiting people within the U.S. to advance their interests.
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE
First Assistant United States Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks as U.S. and Canadian law enforcement officials announce federal charges and arrests of alleged members of a transnational organized crime group at FBI offices in Los Angeles, Calif., on July 7, 2026. (REUTERS)
"They're willing to steal our technology; they're willing to engage in espionage here. So, there's no limit to what China is willing to do. It is a huge, huge concern. We have to be vigilant, and we have to disrupt these operations on our soil," Essayli said. "We have to protect our sovereignty."
"If you look at just the cases we brought this year, just in my office, I mean, you had cases where the woman from Irvine was engaged in espionage against the Taiwanese president's family member . I had a guy last week we arrested, he sold more than $300 million in SI chips, formerly known as AI chips, to China," he continued. "You had a mayor of a local city that we charged for serving as an unregistered agent of China as well, pushing out their propaganda and taking orders from China."
FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US
This photo provided by the Federal Bureau of Investigation shows Wanying Zhang being arrested Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Federal Bureau of Investigation via AP)
"So, it's extremely pervasive. It's a huge problem, but the FBI is on it," he said. "They have entire squads dedicated to combating this, and we're committed here at the U.S. Attorney's Office to supporting those investigations and bringing criminal charges to disrupt these operations."
Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, was arrested earlier this month for allegedly working with an associate to photograph and record the family outside their Seattle-area home, according to a criminal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital.
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
Authorities nabbed Zhang, who goes by "Heather" in the U.S., at the Los Angeles airport as she attempted to board a plane to China.
This undated photo released by the U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, shows Wanying Zhang. (U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California via AP)
Essayli said FBI Los Angeles agents arrested Zhang on a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China.
CALIFORNIA MAYOR ACCUSED OF SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING PROPAGANDA WHILE IN OFFICE: FEDS
She allegedly traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, videos and license plate information.
"She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection," Essayli wrote. "She never notified the attorney general she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense."
GOOGLE ENGINEER STOLE AI SECRETS FOR CHINA, SENATE HEARS IN EXPLOSIVE TESTIMONY
Former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang exits federal court after pleading guilty to acting as an illegal foreign agent on behalf of the Chinese government. (William Liang/Associated Press)
Speaking on "The Big Weekend Show" Sunday, Essayli said Zhang is a naturalized U.S. citizen and confirmed the alleged surveillance targeted a relative of Taiwan’s president.
"She was conducting surveillance on behalf of the Chinese government. She was acting as a foreign agent," Essayli said. "And she was spying on a relative of the president of Taiwan here in the U.S."
The alleged target was Ting-Yu Lai, the U.S.-based son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, CBS News reported , citing law enforcement sources. The complaint does not name him.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli speaks at a Los Angeles press conference announcing developments in a terrorism investigation on Dec. 15, 2025. (Damian Dovarganes/AP)
"Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one," Zhang allegedly messaged a Chinese government contact while outside the home.

"I am video recording," she allegedly added before sending two license plate numbers.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

articles.title_orig: Blindsided again by Trump, Europe scrambles to rally behind Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Blindsided again by Trump, Europe scrambles to rally behind Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Europe is once again trying to save face after US President Donald Trump blindsided the continent by striking a tailored deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to release thousands of tonnes of diesel that had until now been sanctioned.
The news alarmed Ukraine and its European allies, who have long been wary of Trump's unpredictable diplomacy and his understanding of what a just and lasting peace means.
Tensions between the two sides of the Atlantic have never fully receded since February last year, when Trump unexpectedly called Putin and launched negotiations to end the war without consulting any European leader in advance.
That was the start of a series of unexpected developments that have rattled Europe and upended its long-held assumptions about the post-war international order. These include a hastily organised Trump-Putin summit in Alaska, a leaked 28-point plan heavily favourable to Moscow and a sanctions waiver for Russian crude oil.
The diesel deal, announced on Friday on Truth Social, added yet another chapter.
Trump then resorted to a familiar pattern: public attacks against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's legitimacy and calls for fresh elections. Ukraine's constitution bars elections in wartime, a point that Zelenskyy tends to remind Trump.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said to Moscow's applause.
As in previous episodes, Europe finds itself scrambling to close ranks, rally behind Ukraine and make clear that, regardless of what the White House does and says, this side of the Atlantic will stay the agreed course.
"I think we need to be collectively serious. Today, I believe, we have no factual reason to change our position," French President Emmanuel Macron said on Monday.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said emulating the Trump-Putin diesel deal was "out of the question" for Europe, despite rising energy prices.
"Russia will only negotiate seriously under pressure, and that is why we are sticking to our sanctions against Russia," Merz told reporters.
A similar message echoed through Luxembourg as EU foreign ministers met and insisted that the pressure campaign on Moscow would continue unabated. Some openly decried the diesel deal, calling it regrettable and concerning.
Foreign ministers also approved a record-breaking addition of 1,600 names to the sanctions list, half of them linked to the production of ballistic missiles that fall on Ukraine. The contrast between the EU and the US could hardly have been starker.
"We showed unity today on these (1,600) listings," High Representative Kaja Kallas said at the end of the meeting.
"But, of course, it would be much stronger if we had acted together with the US. Our message to the United States is that only pressure works with Russia."
Although the Trump-Putin deal fits a familiar pattern of erratic diplomacy that sidelines European interests, its grim context sets it apart.
The diesel deal comes at a time when Russia is rapidly escalating its attacks against Ukraine, killing scores of civilians and wrecking the levers that sustain the local economy, including power stations, data centres, warehouses and railways.
Russia's blockade in the Black Sea has left Ukrainian farmers unable to send tonnes of grain to their global clients and deprived the state of an essential revenue source.
As economic activity stagnates and material costs pile up, the EU is realising its multibillion-euro lines of support will fall short sometime next year. With the US out of the picture, the burden is set to fall on the European pocket.
The prospect of Russia selling diesel that had until now been sanctioned and making extra money to finance the bombs that rain down on Ukraine is particularly difficult to stomach for Kyiv and its allies. It also raises serious questions about how much the US can be trusted to provide security guarantees for the post-war scenario.
And yet, Europe's collective assessment remains that there is still more to lose than to gain from breaking away from the Americans.
"What we need to do is refocus and redouble our efforts in keeping pressure on Russia," Ireland's Foreign Minister Helen McEntee said on Monday.
"Our priority has to be to maintain that pressure, but also to maintain our channels with the US, because this is not going to be achievable without the support of the US."
Just as news of the diesel deal broke, senior officials from Ukraine, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the European Commission and NATO were in Miami, Florida, for a round of talks hosted by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Trump's special envoys.
The meeting was the first of its kind since the outbreak of the US-Iran war, which has absorbed the White House's foreign policy and relegated Ukraine to the second row.
"We will continue to engage with our partners and also with the US in bringing this war to a close, and the latest example of this has been the talks on Friday in Miami," the Commission's chief spokesperson said, describing the meeting as a "positive step".
Europe initially struggled to secure a seat at the negotiating table as Trump and Putin marched ahead with their private calls. It took months after European countries established the “Coalition of the Willing” for them to be brought into the US-led negotiating process.
The statements from Brussels confirm that retaining a seat at the table where Ukraine’s future as a sovereign state and Europe’s security architecture will be decided takes precedence over any diplomatic slight, however pointed or public.
Zelenskyy, whose country is already suffering blackouts ahead of a winter expected to be the harshest yet of the war, agrees that the transatlantic alliance must prevail, notwithstanding the deals that might be cut behind its back.
"An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social," Zelenskyy said.
"We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together. Europe and the United States."

articles.title_orig: Dow Rises 200 Points, Nasdaq Wavers: China Chip Competition Hits Tech Stocks, Oil Climbs
articles.title_zh: Dow Rises 200 Points, Nasdaq Wavers: China Chip Competition Hits Tech Stocks, Oil Climbs
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
U.S. stocks traded mixed on Monday, with the Dow rising more than 250 points while the Nasdaq Composite fell amid pressure on semiconductor stocks.
Salesforce shares climbed after Bank of America upgraded the stock to 'Buy' from 'Underperform' and raised its price target to $285 from $160.
Micron and SanDisk declined amid concerns about growing competition from China's CXMT.
U.S. equities traded mixed on Monday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average rising more than 200 points while the Nasdaq Composite slipped as Micron Technology (MU) and other chip stocks tumbled on concerns about competition from China's CXMT.
Adding to market pressure, oil prices climbed amid renewed Russia-Ukraine tensions. Investors were also looking ahead to bank earnings, upcoming inflation data, and a Friday speech by Kevin Warsh this week.
See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox
The SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) edged 0.04% lower at the time of writing, the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF (DIA) gained 0.40%, and the Nasdaq-100 tracking Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) slipped as much as 0.60%. Retail sentiment around QQQ on Stocktwits dropped to 'bullish' from 'extremely bullish' over the past day.
The Dow received support from Salesforce (CRM), which rose after Bank of America (BofA) gave it a double upgrade to 'Buy' from 'Underperform' and raised its price target to $285 from $160.
The firm cited improving prospects for Salesforce's artificial intelligence strategy and stated that large companies are unlikely to abandon established software platforms that house their business data and workflows.
The Nasdaq, on the other hand, faced pressure from semiconductor stocks. Concerns that CXMT could pose bigger competition in memory chips weighed on Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK) and other chip companies in the sector. SNDK stock tumbled 5.6% in midday trade, while MU stock fell by around 3%.
Wells Fargo's double downgrade on Adobe (ADBE) also did not help. The firm downgraded the software maker to 'Underweight' from 'Equal Weight' and lowered its price target to $225 from $270. It cited concerns about slowing organic growth and the challenge of meeting Adobe's full-year targets.
The S&P 500, which covers a broader cross-section of large U.S. companies, held relatively steady as gains in some stocks offset losses elsewhere. eBay (EBAY) was among the top gainers, alongside names like Meta Platforms (META) and Biogen (BIIB).
EBAY stock was also among the top-trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing, gaining as much as 5.5% in the midday trade and marking an over-four-month high. The rally came after Morgan Stanley named the company its top pick in the internet sector. Retail sentiment around the shares on the platform trended in 'bullish' territory over the past day.
Cerebras Systems (CBRS) was among the top trending tickers on Stocktwits and one of the market's biggest losers, falling 9.6% in midday trade, extending its decline after a report last week suggested OpenAI was using Nvidia (NVDA) chips rather than Cerebras' hardware for a feature of its latest AI model. CBRS stock hit a record low of $147.77, leaving it at less than half of its $350 IPO price.
Oil prices added another source of uncertainty for investors. West Texas Intermediate crude futures expiring in November rose over 2% to around more than $93 a barrel in midday trade, while Brent crude futures expiring in December also gained around 2% to trade near $107 a barrel.
The most recent uptick comes after renewed attacks on energy infrastructure and questions over an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced by President Donald Trump over the weekend. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had already violated the agreement, raising doubts about whether the arrangement would ease risks to energy supplies.
The United States Oil Fund (USO) rose around 2.3% in midday trade on Monday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the ETF trended in 'bearish' territory over the past day.
Major U.S. banks are also due to report quarterly results this week, while the September consumer price index will offer a fresh reading on inflation and could influence expectations for the Federal Reserve's next policy decision. Kevin Warsh is scheduled to speak later in the week at an International Monetary Fund and World Bank event in Bangkok.
