articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Deadly Houthi attacks keep Saudi airport closed as Trump considers U.S. strikes in Yemen
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Deadly Houthi attacks keep Saudi airport closed as Trump considers U.S. strikes in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night, just moments after a text message sent to residents' mobile phones warned of an aerial threat.
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors," read the message.
Around the same time, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the coalition, wrote in a post on X.
U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals on Monday, "for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," he said in a statement .
"We will not tolerate threats on British soil," said Miliband, who earlier had released a joint statement alongside his counterparts in the U.S., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, which condemned hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
Their statements followed a security incident at the RAF Fairford air base in southern England, which U.K. government leaders and others have attributed to Iran. Iran denied its involvement Monday in comments released by state media.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
The embassy said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events," without specifying how many were arrested or whether they had been released. It noted that Saudi authorities have warned that "filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Several foreign residents in Riyadh have told AFP that acquaintances were detained for filming recent events and sharing the footage on social media.
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in a security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which the U.S. previously used to deploy long-range bombers during the war.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," the Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
That statement followed earlier remarks from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said the incident was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Monday to have struck three supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the last two days.
The IRGC Navy said in its most recent attack on a ship, Monday, "a third non-compliant super-tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire."
It said the tanker had switched off the system that broadcasts a vessel's location in an effort to evade Iranian restrictions on navigating the strait without permission and "disregarded warnings from the IRGC Navy."
The statement warned that "any cooperation by commercial vessels and oil tankers with the invading, plundering American terrorist and smuggling army in the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf region will be met with a decisive response from us."
President Trump and his senior aides have insisted for weeks that a southern route through the strait, skirting close to Oman's coast, is safe and available, and the U.S. military has escorted an increasing number of ships along that route in recent weeks.
Iran rejects that route and demands that all vessels use a northern passage close to its own coastline, seeking permission from its military.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center, which monitors incidents in the region, had not reported any attacks on vessels Monday, but it noted at least two projectiles hitting vessels Sunday.
The foreign ministers of the U.S., the U.K, Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, many in Europe, have released a joint statement condemning hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
The statement came on the heels of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying a recent security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which was until recently home to U.S. long-range bombers, was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
The countries said Monday that they "condemn in the strongest terms Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
Linking the RAF Fairford incident to other recent attacks in Europe "targeting Jewish communities, Iranian journalists, and U.S. interests," the countries said: "Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable."
"Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
The security incident at a British base used by American bombers to strike Iran during the ongoing war was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday.
British police have arrested and then released on bail seven men in connection with the alleged plot. The decision to free the men, whom British police say remain under investigation and monitoring, drew criticism from President Trump , who said in September the incident "might be" linked to Iran.
"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard," Burnham told lawmakers in the U.K. Parliament on Monday.
"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," he added. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams."
Burnham said new sanctions against Iran would be announced.
Saudi Arabia's energy minister said Monday that the kingdom had been tested, but would mount an "equally serious" response to a string of deadly attacks on Riyadh's international airport by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Lethal airport strikes have rocked the world's top oil exporter since last week, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.
Yemen's decade-old civil war , in which a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Houthis, has reignited months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.
"Energy security can't be taken for granted," Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh. "The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."
Operations remained suspended at the sprawling King Khalid International Airport on Riyadh's outskirts Monday after the weekend's deadly Houthi strikes.
CCTV video of the deadliest strike, which killed 13 people on Saturday, released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden flash tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.
Saudi Arabia will continue implementing its economic goals and investing in energy infrastructure, industrial capacity and international partnerships despite the challenges presented by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said Monday.

articles.title_orig: It’s a Real Shame the OnePlus 16 Is Launching Only in China
articles.title_zh: It’s a Real Shame the OnePlus 16 Is Launching Only in China
articles.content_orig:
OnePlus may be dead in most of the world , including the United States and Europe, but that doesn’t mean the company is done making interesting smartphones. In fact, quite the contrary: the OnePlus 16, just unveiled in China, looks pretty great.
The OnePlus 16 runs on Qualcomm’s latest flagship Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chip. It has a 6.78-inch OLED screen, a huge 9,000 mAh battery, and some built-in lights that show a set of galactic coordinates, as The Verge notes . These lights also alert the user to incoming calls, messages, and other notifications. It’s not just neat but practically pointless space-related numbers.
The space theme also shows up in the phone’s colorways: Starlight, Martian Masterpiece, and Dark Forest, which admittedly has nothing to do with space.
The OnePlus 16’s overall design aesthetic carries forward quite a bit from last year’s OnePlus 15 , a somewhat disappointing end to OnePlus’ time as a global smartphone brand. After the excellent OnePlus 13 used Hasselblad-branded cameras to great effect , it was a shame to see the brand fall from grace with the OnePlus 15. It was fine, but felt like a step back in the camera department.
OnePlus hopes to right the ship a bit with the 16. It has a 200-megapixel main camera with a Type 1/1.4 image sensor and a 23mm equivalent f/1.6 lens. This is a big change from the OnePlus 15’s 50-megapixel main camera with a 24mm f/1.8 lens. The 15’s main camera featured a Type 1/1.56 sensor, by the way.
The 200MP primary camera is flanked by a 50-megapixel telephoto with a Type 1/1.95 sensor, 73mm equivalent lens, and f/2.6 aperture. There’s also a 50-megapixel 116° ultrawide camera with a relatively small Type 1/2.88 sensor.
While the ultrawide camera is unchanged, the telephoto looks like a step up. The lens is a bit shorter — 73mm versus 80mm equivalent — but it’s faster (f/2.6 versus f/2.8). The image sensor is also considerably larger. The OnePlus 15’s telephoto camera featured a Type 1/2.76 sensor.
Unfortunately, most of the world will not get to enjoy the OnePlus 16. For now, the device is launching exclusively in China, starting at 5,699 Chinese yuan, or around $850. OnePlus may have an exciting new smartphone on offer, but the company has still officially exited the North American and European markets.

articles.title_orig: Middaugh wins world title at XTERRA championships in New Mexico
articles.title_zh: Middaugh wins world title at XTERRA championships in New Mexico
articles.content_orig:
Two-time XTERRA short-track world champion Sullivan Middaugh earned his first full-distance world title at XTERRA’s 30th World Championship over the weekend in Ruidoso, New Mexico.
Middaugh, of EagleVail, won in 2:06:50, finishing five minutes and 56 seconds ahead of Spain’s Nacho Gálvez. Denmark’s Jens Emil Sloth Nielsen took third.
At Grindstone Lake, the water temperature was 64.6°F (18.1°C), while the air temperature was 53.2°F (11.8°C) an hour before the start. At Wingfield Park, morning temperatures were around 59°F (15°C), with a high near 70°F (21°C).
The course began with a 1.5K swim before climbing into rocky singletrack on a single 27K mountain-bike lap. Riders crossed the high terrain around Grindstone Mesa before descending toward the village. The final 10K run took athletes through village streets and forest trails, returning through Wingfield Park between the two laps and into the finish.
Gálvez led out of Grindstone Lake in 18:21, followed closely by Sullivan and Porter Middaugh. Sullivan felt comfortable in the water and wanted to reach the singletrack first, knowing Sloth Nielsen would be chasing from behind.
Both leaders described falls early on the bike. Gálvez crashed on the first corner, while Middaugh fell on the third and lost his bike computer.
“I think it was maybe a blessing in disguise not to have power data,” Middaugh said. “I just rode how I was feeling and rode as hard as I could the whole time.”
His 1:07:18 bike split was the fastest in the elite men’s field. He carried his advantage into the run and added another leading split of 39:00.
“I knew that at altitude I could run uphill just as fast as anyone else,” he said. “So I pushed every climb, let it roll on every descent, and just gave it everything I could.”
Gálvez kept chasing after his fall and held second through the run. “But I never lost faith,” he said. “On the run, I gave everything I had, and I was able to finish second. I’m super happy.”
Sloth Nielsen worked forward from thirteenth at bike start to complete the podium, crediting the preparation of the two athletes ahead of him. “Sullivan and Nacho must have just prepared better,” he said. “They’ve been at altitude for longer.”
Arthur Serrières finished fourth, followed by Maxim Chané. Josiah Middaugh placed sixth and Porter seventh, putting all three Middaughs inside the top ten.
“Just a proud day,” Josiah said. “Really happy for Sullivan. Start to finish, he just put it together.”
Porter finished after a heavy bike crash and described racing alongside his father as both inspiring and helpful in getting him through the course.
XTERRA had been part of childhood for the Middaugh brothers before it became a championship ambition.
“It means everything. It’s how we grew up, watching our dad and going to races with him,” Sullivan said.
He also remembered Arthur Serrières encouraging him after his first Worlds in Maui in 2021. “I remember Arthur telling me at the dinner afterwards to stick with it,” he said. “At that point, he was already a world champion, so that meant a lot.”

articles.title_orig: Zelensky says strikes on Ukraine infrastructure 'Putin's answer' to Trump on energy ceasefire
articles.title_zh: Zelensky says strikes on Ukraine infrastructure 'Putin's answer' to Trump on energy ceasefire
articles.content_orig:
President Zelensky says strikes on Ukraine's infrastructure are "Putin's answer" to Donald Trump, after the US president claimed a Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" was in place
In a post on X, Zelensky says "last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on the territory of Russia... while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities"
"The message from Russia was very clear - they don't know anything about the energy ceasefire," Zelensky adds
Asked earlier about Trump's announcement, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said "as soon as we have something to say on the matter, we will inform you"
Meanwhile, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Kyiv doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring
Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure so Moscow can fulfil a recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices
Edited by Charlotte Hadfield
Ukraine has reported further Russian strikes after US President Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Kyiv and Moscow.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had hit six energy facilities in Ukraine despite the announcement.
Zelensky, who said he was surprised by the news , said that the ceasefire could "become a major step toward ending the war".
He also responded to Trump's calls for a Ukrainian election by stating that to do so, a "full ceasefire" would be required.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters on Monday that he does not believe Zelensky "deserves a respite" from the war.
Meanwhile, Trump has appeared to defend his recently -announced plan to import diesel from Russia , writing on Truth Social that the EU had "paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy" adding he "made the right choice" for Americans.
Russia's latest attacks on Ukraine seem to have justified Ukrainian concerns that the US had struck a diesel deal with Russia without securing anything in return, adds BBC News Russian's Liza Fokht .
We're pausing our live coverage, but you can read more in our news story.
This isnât the first time US President Donald Trump has announced an energy ceasefire.
On 14 September he posted: âUkraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!â
The day before, Trump had said Ukraineâs attacks on Russian oil and gas facilities were âhurting the worldâ and urged Zelensky to stop targeting Russian refineries.
He said he spoke to Zelensky and told him âyou gotta take it easy on the refineriesâ.
Since then Ukraine has carried out 14 strikes on 13 different refineries, including twice in Moscow, while Russia has continued to strike energy facilities in Ukraine.
On 18 March 2025, Trump got Putin and Zelensky to agree that for 30 days they would "not strike energy infrastructure facilities".
But within days Moscow and Kyiv were accusing each other of having "broken" the ceasefire and it didn't last.
French President Emmanuel Macron
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said Russia would only negotiate "seriously" under pressure, days after Donald Trump announced a temporary easing of US sanctions on Russian diesel. As a result, Merz says Europe will be "maintaining our sanctions against Russia".
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he welcomes Trump's "announcement yesterday of a reciprocal energy ceasefire", telling the House of Commons that President Zelensky "has assured me Ukraine would immediately implement it when a start date is confirmed".
French President Emmanuel Macron says he's not noticed "any energy ceasefire from the Russian side", adding there can only be progress "if there is a real truce which is respected by both sides".
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk told the Warsaw Security Forum earlier that every time a ceasefire is proposed to Russia "to stop bombing critical infrastructure, to cease bombing civilian facilities", it's met with a "brutal and arrogant answer".
Estonia Prime Minister Kristen Michal has posted on X saying "Russia continues to bomb Ukraine's energy infrastructure", and the EU must "stay the course and cut Russia's energy revenues".
European Council President Antonio Costa says "no one wants peace more than Ukraine", announcing that EU members adopted "nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russiaâs military-industrial complex".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz
Daniel Bush Washington correspondent
The chances of President Trump responding to President Zelensky's remarks earlier are probably not very high.
Trump did criticise Zelensky over the weekend, saying that Ukraine needed a new leader to negotiate a deal.
Trump has been unwilling at times to hear out Zelensky, often blaming him for the war and the inability of Ukraine and Russia to end the conflict.
The US president has tried to cast a wide net of blame for high gas prices, while arguing that theyâre not his fault and will come down soon. Weâve heard that rhetoric from Trump before.
Zelenskyâs comments appeared aimed at countering that by reminding the world â and Americans â that the war with Iran has driven up the cost of oil and gas.
Polling shows that Americans are certainly very concerned about that issue. Whether or not Zelensky's message to them will resonate is unclear.
Speaking at a conference in Warsaw earlier today, Ukranian President Zelensky said what Ukraine needs is "American pressure on Russia, not sanctions relief, not concessions, but real pressure".
He noted that "immediately after" Donald Trump's assertion on Sunday that he had brokered an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, Russia hit a plant in Kharkiv.
These are some of the latest images coming to us from Kharkiv, Sloviansk and the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv as strikes continue.
The scene of a fire at a residential building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kharkiv
A firefighter kneels amid smoke and debris at the site of a Russian drone attack in the Darnytskyi district of Kyiv
A resident searches for documents in the ruins of houses destroyed following a Russian guided aerial bomb attack in Kharkiv
A doctor treats a woman following a Russian airstrike on a residential building in Sloviansk
Mitchell Labiak BBC Business reporter
The global benchmark oil price has risen despite US President Donald Trump's attempt to drive the price down with his agreement to buy Russian oil.
The cost of contracts to purchase a barrel of Brent crude one month from now, known as futures, climbed over 2% on Monday to $107 (Â£81).
Brent crude futures were priced at around $70 (Â£53) a barrel before the start of the US-Israel war with Iran but shot up after the conflict started, with the fighting having severely disrupted the production and transportation of energy in the region.
Brent crude futures tend to drop following signs that there might be an end to the fighting and rise when conflict tensions increase.
This has fed through to higher costs for car fuel in many countries, including the US where prices at the pump are a big complaint from voters ahead of the midterm elections.
Trump has responded to this by making several announcements aimed at reducing oil prices, but analysts have warned that his deal to buy oil from Russia would not have a noticeable impact.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says last night they didn't attack Russian energy facilities "because President Trump said that there would be an energy ceasefire".
In a post on X , external , which he attributes to an interview with Fox News, Zelensky adds: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities.
"I think it was Putinâs answer to President Trump."
He says the message from Russia is clear: "They don't know anything about the energy ceasefire", as he calls for more pressure on Russia.

articles.title_orig: RIT student’s designs will help power world’s first Electron-Ion Collider
articles.title_zh: RIT student’s designs will help power world’s first Electron-Ion Collider
articles.content_orig:
Scott Hamilton/ RIT Photography
RIT student Robert Desjardins designed the four-tiered storage system to hold the superconducting magnets that will be installed in the new Electron-Ion Collider at Brookhaven Laboratory.
When the U.S. Department of Energy’s Brookhaven National Laboratory needed multiple stands that could each support up to 45,000 pounds of superconducting magnets in limited space, a Rochester Institute of Technology student designed the solution.
Fourth-year mechanical engineering technology student Robert Desjardins spent his summer internship redesigning storage stands that will help Brookhaven prepare for the world's first Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), a next-generation particle accelerator that will help scientists understand the building blocks of matter.
During his 10-week internship, Desjardins developed a four-level design capable of safely storing 20-foot-long magnets weighing more than 10,000 pounds each. The stands will allow magnets being removed from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), in service for more than 26 years at Brookhaven, to be stored for reuse on the new Electron-Ion Collider, which is expected to become operational in the mid-2030s.
“The original stands were designed in the 1990s, and at the time they could hold only three of the magnets. They wanted to up the capacity to four,” said Desjardins. “I had to get my project fully designed, look at blueprints, revise computer-aided models, and start talking to the manufacturers and simulate some of the strength tests required.”
RIT alumnus and Brookhaven mechanical engineer Jonathon Greene '15 ( mechanical engineering ), who helped oversee the project, served as Desjardins’s mentor during the internship.
David Rahner/Brookhaven National Laboratory
RIT alumnus Jonathon Greene, right, and Desjardins are pictured in front of the new four-tier magnet storage stand Desjardins designed. Greene, who has been at Brookhaven National Laboratory since 2022, mentored Desjardins through his internship. They are standing next to a superconducting magnet.
In an article written by the lab, Greene credits Desjardins’s work with significant project savings. “Rob costed down the original design while increasing the height. We saved about $420,000 by doing so.”
Greene said he expects about 80 magnets will come out of RHIC and need to be stored for the EIC using Desjardins’s design.
During the prototype development, Desjardins met regularly with Greene and presented status information to the larger group of project engineers and scientists, fielding tough questions about materials, status of safety reviews, and results of simulations testing for load capacity and even seismic analysis.
“In engineering you have to simulate for the worst at all times. I did so many simulations; the design was half the project. The other half was performing the simulations and checking my work,” said Desjardins, who is from West Sayville, N.Y., and is also working on a master’s degree in mechatronics and mechanical systems in RIT’s College of Engineering Technology .
Both Greene and Desjardins attribute some success in the field to participating on co-ops and internships that provide students with real-world experience. Technical coursework in 3D modeling, strength of materials, and load tolerance are foundational concepts for engineers. These were the skills Desjardins said he learned at RIT and brought to the Brookhaven project.
RIT’s renowned internship and co-op program , one of the oldest and largest in the nation, allows students to learn on the job and define their career paths. More than 4,000 RIT students completed co-ops or internships last year, engaging in paid work experience at national and global companies and organizations in nearly every industry.
“This was such a great experience, to learn and hear feedback on a project from experienced engineers, experts at their craft, and to be part of such a huge international project,” said Desjardins. “This was all real teamwork and it was great.”

articles.title_orig: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford Awarded Nobel for Economics
articles.title_zh: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford Awarded Nobel for Economics
articles.content_orig:
Monday, October 12, 2026 80° Today's Paper
Today • Last updated
                                            8:43 a.m.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are announced as the laureates of the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden, today.
STOCKHOLM >> U.S. academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.
“With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.
Woodford and Hall are frequently name-checked by the world’s top central banks, which after a 2022 inflation surge in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, are currently grappling with the energy shock triggered by the Iran war.
One of the laureates’ key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.
“… Authorities shouldn’t view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this,” Columbia University’s Woodford, 70, told a news conference.
In contrast to the oil shocks of the 1970s, when central banks struggled to combat sky-high inflation, Woodford said the new framework was useful during the global financial crisis of the late-2000s to bolster traditional tools of monetary policy.
Stay in touch with breaking news, as it happens, conveniently in your email inbox. It's FREE!
“Making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy, as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately, that was an important part of the policy response in the years from 2009 onward,” he said.
Beyond so-called “forward guidance” on the future path of monetary policy, the work of Woodford — and Hall, 83, at Stanford University — promoted other concepts used today such as the idea of “sticky” inflation when price changes lag changes in demand.
Another is the “output gap,” a measure of demand pressure building up in an economy and how efficiently resources are being used — the goal of stabilisation policy being to steer that gap towards zero.
Hall has served as adviser to the U.S. Treasury Department, the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve Board.
His insight in a 1978 paper that household decisions on consumption are a perfect indicator of their expectations was used by Woodford in a model on how consumption is determined.
Woodford also showed that central banks can stimulate or suppress economic activity by adjusting interest rates, rather than just by the amount of money in circulation.
Such concepts remain core to central banking today. Forward guidance became especially important after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were near zero or even negative and standard monetary policy seemed to be out of ammunition.
Now, however, some are questioning how relevant it is given the amount of uncertainty in the global economy — with new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh a notable sceptic.
The economics prize, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final award to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).
First awarded in 1969, it is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden’s central bank.
The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.
Last year’s winners, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on “creative destruction” and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.
The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last week.
Reporting by Simon Johnson, Niklas Pollard, Johan Ahlander and Marie Mannes in Stockholm, Terje Solsvik in Oslo, Mark John in London.

articles.title_orig: You can now start the iPhone Duo pre-order process

articles.content_orig:
iPhone Duo pre-orders officially kick off on Friday, but Apple is letting you prepare now . Starting today, you can head to the Apple Store Online or Apple Store app and save your exact iPhone Duo configuration.
Apple has offered this “get ready for pre-order” window for the last several years. It allows you to streamline the pre-order process by preparing key details ahead of time. This includes the iPhone Duo color, storage, and carrier options.
You can also prepare your iPhone Duo pre-order payment method. You can pay in full, finance with Apple Card, join the Apple Upgrade program, or check for applicable carrier offers.
Completed. Earlier, I considered securing a 12-month lease by trading in the iPhone 17 Pro Max for $885; however, that approach would have been disadvantageous. The total cost would have amounted to $885 plus $9.95 per month for 12 months—$1,182.20—with no residual value after the term. Instead, I opted for a trade-in with Apple Card financing. After 12 months, I expect to trade in this device pair, apply the proceeds toward the remaining balance, and upgrade to a new model. The outcomes may appear similar, but the financial structure is more favorable.
If you complete this process ahead of time, you can check out in just a couple of taps when iPhone Duo pre-orders officially begin on Friday morning.
The new “get ready” option is available today and will likely run through much of the day on Friday, October 15. You’ll then have to return to the Apple Store app or website on Friday, October 16 at 5 a.m. PT/8 a.m. ET to finalize your order.

articles.title_orig: Oil rally pressures S&P, Nasdaq; Microsoft, Salesforce buoy Dow
articles.title_zh: Oil rally pressures S&P, Nasdaq; Microsoft, Salesforce buoy Dow
articles.content_orig:
The S&P 500 was little changed on Monday after the major averages posted a winning week and as investors looked ahead to a busy week of earnings results and inflation data.
The broad market index traded down 0.1%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, trading up 177 points, or 0.3%. The Nasdaq Composite , however, was 0.5% lower.
The Nasdaq was weighed down by a 3% drop in shares of Micron Technology . The move came as investors assessed increasing competition from China's CXMT , which reported progress on a new chip structure . In contrast, the Dow was boosted by a more than 1% rise in Salesforce shares after the name received a double upgrade at Bank of America .
Meanwhile, oil prices rose after President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, then Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow had already violated it . West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 2% to around $94 per barrel. Brent crude gained 2% to trade at $107 per barrel.
Trump also told reporters he was considering joining Saudi Arabia in its fight against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after another deadly attack on Riyadh's international airport. The remarks raised the prospect of escalating tensions in the region.
Wall Street is coming off a winning week for the major averages, as a rally in tech stocks helped investors shrug off higher oil prices and yields. The Dow and S&P 500 each posted their second positive week in three, while the Nasdaq netted its fourth straight week of gains.
Investors hope the third-quarter earnings season will help stocks power through the Middle East turmoil. By all estimations, the incoming results are expected to be strong. According to FactSet's John Butters, the S&P 500 is set to post 29.6% earnings growth in the quarter. That would be the fourth straight quarter that the broader index posts above-25% earnings growth, thanks to the strength of the AI data center buildout.
The reporting season will ramp up in earnest this week with the big banks, with Bank of America , Citigroup , Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase , Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo all expected to post results this week.
Key inflation data is due out this week as well, with the September consumer and producer price indexes due out Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
"It's going to be all on earnings," Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion, said to CNBC. He added that even if this week's inflation prints are hotter than expected, the market is going to regard them as "not enough to derail" the Federal Reserve, which is largely expected to keep interest rates steady at its next meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool .
"Something will upend this bull market at some point, but I think the most important thing going on right now is the AI capex buildout," he said.
This week marks four years since the start of the S&P 500's bull run after the index notched a closing low of 3,577.03 in October 2022. Since then, the index has more than doubled.
— CNBC's Terri Cullen contributed to this report.
Morgan Stanley downgraded Ally Financial to equal weight on Monday as higher rates pressure the online bank's earnings.
"We now forecast less earnings upside amid higher interest rates and a less favorable credit backdrop," analyst Jeffrey Adelson said in a note to clients.
While he is not calling for a material contraction in net interest margin or a worsening in auto credit, he believes those to key earnings drivers are unlikely to improve much from here. That will keep a lid on return on tangible common equity, which is a measure of a bank's profitability,  and earnings-per-share growth for now, Adelson added.
The State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) touched an intraday all-time high on Monday – its first in more than a month.
The XLE last traded more than 1% higher. It last hit a record on Sept. 10.
The ETF jumped as international Brent crude futures took a leg higher, rising about 2% to trade above $106 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained more than 2% to trade just below $94.
Stocks leading the XLE higher include Diamondback Energy , Oneok , APA and ConocoPhillips , all of which were up around 2%.
— Darla Mercado and Gina Francolla
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said Monday that tighter monetary policy might be needed to bring down inflation and the central bank should make fast, incremental adjustments.
"When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," Hammack, a voting member of the Fed's policymaking committee, said in prepared remarks delivered during the National Association of Business Economics annual gathering.
"Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation," Hammack added.
Read the full story here .
All but two S&P 500 sectors were in the green in midday trading on Monday.
Energy and communication services led the way, with both rising about 1.4%. Consumer staples followed suit, gaining 0.8%.
Information technology and consumer discretionary were the two sectors in negative territory. The former was down around 0.9%, while the latter fell 0.5%.
The broad market index was last trading just below the flatline.
AST SpaceMobile , the company pioneering space-based mobile broadband, is a buy on weakness, according to Deutsche Bank.
The bank upgraded the stock to buy from hold and maintained its $93 price target. That implies upside of 82% from Friday's close.
Shares are down more than 26% year to date, and they dropped 10% on Friday after Elon Musk said SpaceX would buy a nationwide spectrum portfolio, which would allow the space company to compete with mobile providers. However, the stock climbed around 5% on Monday following the upgrade.
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
RBC Capital Markets sees some risks entering in the third quarter reporting season.
The firm cited risks including the effects Iran war, the possibility that 2027 earnings per share forecasts are too high, midterm elections, and the Fed's new hiking cycle.
Therefore, it noted S&P 500 earnings per share outlook could contribute to a short-term pullback.
Global shipping stocks reached a new set of all time highs shortly after the open off of increased oil shipping prices.
Global Shipping ETF hit yet another all-time high at the opening bell, and many stocks of companies that ship oil and gas including Torm PLC , Hafina and Teekay Tankers opened at fresh 52-week highs.
As CNBC's Brian Sullivan reports, high costs to ship oil amid continued tensions in the Middle East are adding "premiums" to the complete price of oil on top of Brent and WTI crude futures. Both Brent and WTI crude are trading at their highest levels in over two weeks Monday morning.
U.S. equities were relatively unchanged on Monday morning.
The S&P 500 rose 0.1% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 83 points, or about 0.2%. The Nasdaq Composite was 0.1% lower.
Starbucks said on Monday that it is not considering a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill , with a Starbucks spokesperson telling CNBC that the company is "not buying Chipotle."
Shares of the coffee giant were more than 1% higher in premarket trading following the denial, while Chipotle shares were down more than 2%.
— Amelia Lucas and Sean Conlon
Salesforce could get a much-needed boost as it integrates artificial intelligence into its businesses, according to Bank of America.
The bank double upgraded the stock to buy from underperform. It also raised its price target to $285 from $160, which is 24% above the level at which shares last closed.

The World Council of Churches (WCC) shared warm greetings upon the celebration of the 60th Jubilee of Focolare ’ s arrival in Sweden, and then to all of Scandinavia.
“ To me, the particular gift and genius of Focolare—and a forward edge of the ecumenical movement—lies in its unique combination of ecumenical Christian spirituality and living in community that transcends boundaries,” reads a letter from WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay. “ That faith-filled orientation, that commitment, that way of life, holds profound potential as a model and catalyst for Christians everywhere and for the world.”
Pillay commended the Focolare ’ s communal witness. “ So, my friends, as you gather in fellowship, may your time together spark fresh creativity and commitment to the environment and care for the earth, peacebuilding, interreligious encounter, living in community, and deepening our love for God, each other, and all creation,” Pillay concluded. “ May the Spirit whose love fills the universe be also the source of the creative energy we need to realize that vision.”

articles.title_orig: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'
articles.title_zh: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism .
Trump, in a Truth Social post , accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union.
"The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote.
While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy.
"I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.
Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months.
The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin , ends the war against Ukraine.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.
Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal.
"While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.
Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent , however.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

articles.title_orig: Yorkshire Wildlife Park fatal tiger attack - what we know so far
articles.title_zh: Yorkshire Wildlife Park fatal tiger attack - what we know so far
articles.content_orig:
Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster remains closed after a man died in the tiger enclosure on Saturday.
Here's what we know so far about the attack.
Yorkshire Wildlife Park was busy with visitors when the alarm was raised on Saturday afternoon.
Emergency services were called to the park at about 13:30 BST to reports a man had climbed into the tiger enclosure from a high walkway.
Visitors were moved away from the area as the tiger attacked the man, who died a short time later.
The park confirmed the rare Amur tiger, called Altai, remained safely in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.
The park was closed on Saturday and has not yet reopened .
Yorkshire Wildlife Park spans 150 acres with 15 unique habitats featuring wide paths and raised viewing areas.
It focuses on large animal conservation, and counts species including lions, meerkats, lemurs, African penguins and sea lions among its residents.
The tigers are housed in the park's Land of the Tigers, which has a 300m-long raised walkway so visitors can watch the animals from above.
The park's website says people can witness the "majestic cats freely roaming their woodlands and grasslands or playing in their very own waterfall pool".
The man has not been named, but eyewitnesses described seeing a man in his 20s on the walkway at the tiger enclosure, wearing headphones and "pacing around" minutes before the incident took place.
South Yorkshire Police confirmed he was visiting the park on his own.
Speaking to the BBC, Ella Ford, 24, from Wirral, said she saw the same man had climbed up onto the barriers and was spoken to by a woman before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".
Ford said she then saw the man shouting for help and the tiger grabbed hold of him.
She estimates about 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.
People nearby were confused, she said, and one man was "trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything".
Altai is a rare Amur tiger, also known as a Siberian tiger, the largest big cat in the world.
According to the park, the average weight for males is 160-190kg (25-30 stone), while females are smaller, at 110-130kg (17-20 stone).
Altai, now five years old, moved to Yorkshire Wildlife Park from Dyreparken in Norway in February 2025.
The tiger was moved to Doncaster as part of the international EAZA European Endangered Species Programme for Amur tigers, to join the park's resident tigress Tschuna.
Dyreparken biologist Helene Axelsen said: "We were deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park over the weekend.
"Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim's family, loved ones, and the entire team at Yorkshire Wildlife Park during this extremely difficult time."
A spokesperson for the park thanked everyone who showed concern after the incident.
In a statement on Sunday, they said: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies remain with the family and loved ones of the man who tragically lost his life.
"The park will be closed today and the staff team who were deeply affected by events will receive specialist support.
"Many, many people have contacted us about Altai, the tiger.
"We can reassure everyone that he is safe and well and will not be euthanised as a result of this incident."
Dr David Sands, a human-companion animal practitioner at the Animal Behavioural Clinic in Chorley, Lancashire, said tigers were predators that would naturally attack.
"The animal is just being the animal that a million years of evolution has produced," he said.
"It is the top apex predator of its group of animals.
"I don't think any blame could be put on the animal itself."
He added: "Tigers are territorial. This is a male tiger and the incredible weight and power, there's only one outcome because the tiger is in captivity - the enclosure is its territory and a male who can be scented becomes either competition or prey.
"We're so used to seeing them on the small screen in wildlife documentaries.
"This is a very big animal that's got the power to bite and break through bones."
City of Doncaster Council confirmed a health and safety investigation had been launched into the death of the man in the enclosure.
Dan Swaine, the local authority's executive director of place, said the council was "deeply saddened" by the incident and sent its "deepest sympathies" to the man's family and those who were at the scene.
"As the relevant licensing authority for the Yorkshire Wildlife Park, I can confirm that, in line with our statutory duties, the council has launched a health and safety investigation," he said.
"We are also working with multiple agencies, including the police and health agencies, and are supporting the Yorkshire Wildlife Park in response to the incident."

Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch.
Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls.
Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule.
It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)
Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides, and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.
The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.
Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters.
The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27.
Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99.

articles.title_orig: She broke a Guinness record by accident. Then this St. Louis Park woman doubled down, on purpose.
articles.title_zh: She broke a Guinness record by accident. Then this St. Louis Park woman doubled down, on purpose.
articles.content_orig:
A St. Louis Park, Minnesota, woman broke a Guinness World Record Sunday for rucking a half marathon while carrying a 40 pound pack.
Megan Corey ran the half marathon in two hours and three minutes. The previous record was two hours and 20 minutes. Corey also beat the record for the 20 pound ruck during the same race in Dundas.
"First time going for a Guinness World Record," said Corey. "I found out about the Guinness World Record for the fastest half marathon for females carrying a pack when I did a half marathon in Tennessee last year and it was a 20 pound pack half marathon. And found out after from a fellow racer that I had broken the 20 pound record, unbeknownst to me. But you have to predeclare. So today I'm predeclaring and going for the 40 pound record."
The previous 20 pound record was two hours and 34 minutes.

articles.title_orig: Several days of destructive waves from Tropical Storm Rachel leave 8 buildings red-tagged in Long Beach
articles.title_zh: Several days of destructive waves from Tropical Storm Rachel leave 8 buildings red-tagged in Long Beach
articles.content_orig:
Inspectors are assessing damaged homes between Long Beach high tides.
LONG BEACH, Calif. (KABC) -- Destructive waves from the remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel continued crashing into homes on the Long Beach Peninsula for a fourth day, leaving several properties on the verge of ruin and inspectors with limited time to assess the damage before the next high tide.
Eight buildings along the boardwalk have been red-tagged so far, affecting 13 individual addresses, while one building has been yellow-tagged. The number could change as inspectors get a closer look at the damage.
Crews had a small window of daylight between Sunday night’s high tide and another high tide coming in around 10 a.m. Monday to inspect the homes and determine whether additional buildings needed to be red-tagged. They will have another brief window before Monday night’s high tide.
Video from overnight shows worsening damage from the relentless waves, including smashed windows and doors. The destruction extends beyond the exteriors of the homes, with waves washing away sand from beneath the buildings and potentially shifting their foundations.
One home had a crack stretching from its foundation to the roof, and the front half of the building appeared to have shifted.
“As the waves are hitting these structures, it's pulling the soil away from the foundations and the substructures of these buildings, potentially undermining the foundations of these buildings,” said Dan Fox, president of the Structural Engineers Association of Southern California.
A mandatory evacuation order remains in place for residents on 64th and 65th streets along Seaside Walk.
“Long Beach is on sand, right? We’re built on sand. If the ocean gets far enough into the structures where the sand sits, it sucks it out. This is what happens,” Long Beach resident Gabriella Holt said. “I’ve lived here 12 years and have never seen anything... even just this collapse.”
Some of the sand berms built along the beach in an effort to protect homes have completely washed away.
Neighbors told Eyewitness News that although they place sandbags and prepare for high surf and flooding each year, they were not mentally prepared for this level of destruction.

articles.title_orig: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
articles.title_zh: 2 American economists win Nobel for work on managing economic shocks
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

A new report by Securities Times in China indicates Apple is now anticipating much higher demand for iPhone Duo than initially expected, despite pre-orders not starting until later this week.
Apple launches iPhone Duo pre-orders this Friday, October 16. And you’ll be able to start your pre-order process for the fastest checkout later today .
But despite pre-orders not being live yet, Apple seems to be anticipating significantly higher demand for iPhone Duo than its initial estimates.
According to a report from China’s Securities Times , Apple has increased its orders for iPhone Duo in the supply chain by a massive 30%.
The report says total supply for the remainder of 2026 still doesn’t exceed 10 million units. But based on prior estimates of 6-7 million units being produced, it’s likely that the new target number is close to 10 million.
Clearly, Apple is seeing a better than expected response to the iPhone Duo since its unveiling last month. And its planned retail push adds more evidence to support that.
Supply chain sources also tell Securities Times that iPhone 18 Pro Max orders have increased by 10-15% and iPhone 18 Pro orders have been reduced by 10-15%. The total supply targets for the iPhone 18 Pro line overall are ultimately unchanged, however, contradicting a recent Nikkei Asia report .

articles.title_orig: World War II notes linked to ‘The Great Escape’ prison camp found in garage crawlspace
articles.title_zh: World War II notes linked to ‘The Great Escape’ prison camp found in garage crawlspace
articles.content_orig:
A man in upstate New York discovered more than cobwebs and missing holiday decorations while recently cleaning out his garage. Behind a small wood plank, homeowner Jason Hurdle spotted a long-forgotten crawlspace stuffed with vintage milk pails, a safe, and a dusty box of files . Hurdle intended to simply toss the papers in the trash, until a perfectly timed gust of wind removed the crate’s lid. Only then did he realize the box’s true contents: dozens of reports labeled “Secret” relating to Stalag Luft 3, an infamous prison camp run by the Nazi Luftwaffe near Germany’s western border during World War II . Over 300 pages of handwritten accounts from U.S. soldiers recounting their brutal incarcerations at the facility under conditions “not fit for humans.”
“I feel the hurt, the pain, and a lot of things these guys have been through,” Hurdle recently told local news outlet WHEC .
A visit from specialists at the National Archives quickly confirmed the authenticity of the questionnaires, which were compiled in 1945 following Allied liberations of German POW camps. The box was clearly intended for use as evidence of war crimes, which the reports corroborate in tragic detail. Soldiers wrote about living in facilities with “no heat, no beds” while exposed to the elements and vermin. Other troops recalled grueling work on rail lines while witnessing beatings, executions, and even the “cold blooded murder” of surrendering armed forces. Stalag Luft 3 is famously the site of a breakout later recounted by former prisoner Paul Brickhill in the book and 1963 film adaptation, The Great Escape .
“When I first laid them on the table in front of them, the first thing the one agent said was, ‘These are original, we want these,’” added Hurdle.
It’s still unclear how the box ended up inside the garage crawlspace. Hurdle suspects they may have belonged to a retired U.S. Army officer who once lived next door, especially since the box also contained other personal items from the man’s family. In any case, the indispensable historical accounts are now under the care of the National Archives, who have since digitized and unclassified the reports. The entirety of the discovery is now available online to the public.

articles.title_orig: How the Cadillac Formula 1® car communicates with engineers around the world in real time
articles.title_zh: How the Cadillac Formula 1® car communicates with engineers around the world in real time
articles.content_orig:
The cars that compete in Formula 1® are unlike any other race cars on earth. They’re like a supercomputer on wheels, gathering massive amounts of data in real time – and sending it to engineers around the world. Those experts use that information to fine-tune the car in pursuit of every last iota of speed and performance.
On the latest episode of GM’s YouTube Series “What Makes Fast,” we get an inside look into exactly how that data is collected, and how it’s shared with engineers around the globe as the car is competing on the track.
The physical side of this is astounding. One expert estimates there could be more than 10 miles of wiring contained inside the Cadillac Formula 1® Team MAC-26 race car, all of it tasked with measuring and communicating the performance of each vehicle component down to the millisecond. Sensors measure the engine’s power output, the tire pressures, even the speed of the air moving around the vehicle as it streaks down the track. The tiniest change in direction is measured, recorded, and broadcast to experts at the track and between the engineering headquarters in Silverstone, England and Charlotte, North Carolina.
This data doesn’t just tell the racing engineers how the car is performing in the moment. It also guides them as they decide to make adjustments to the car – either in real-time during the race, or in preparation for the next competition. That data is also fed into the highly-accurate GM “Driver In Loop” simulator in Charlotte that the team uses to practice and prepare for the next race.
It’s a high-pressure job. “It’s definitely a weight on our shoulders,” says Ryan Tincher, IT Operations Manager at GM Motorsports. “But it’s not anything the team shies away from… it’s part of what brings everybody back every weekend.”

articles.title_orig: Why IonQ Is Betting Big on Quantum Cybersecurity With $1.3 Billion Elisity Acquisition
articles.title_zh: Why IonQ Is Betting Big on Quantum Cybersecurity With $1.3 Billion Elisity Acquisition
articles.content_orig:
College Park, Md. - Oct. 12, 2026 - IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Elisity, Inc., a Zero Trust security company, in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion. The acquisition brings together IonQ's post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities with Elisity's enterprise Zero Trust technology platform. On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.
Elisity builds on IonQ’s expanding quantum security offerings with a high-growth enterprise security business, cutting-edge Zero Trust technology platform, and team of industry leaders led by cybersecurity expert CEO James Winebrenner. Elisity has a strong track record of doubling its revenue and its customer base year-over-year with zero churn among deployed customers. With more than 100 global customer deployments and deep CISO and security community relationships, Elisity will provide IonQ with expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation opportunity with double-digit CAGR to IonQ.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ, we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity. Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.
“Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” said James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate post-quantum cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.”
Elisity’s Commercial Advantage
Enterprises face two overlapping priorities: containing attacks that operate at machine speed and preparing to protect sensitive information against future quantum threats. The urgency of this transition is underscored by recent White House executive orders advancing quantum innovation and accelerating the federal government's migration to PQC. These directives reinforce the importance of securing critical systems and preparing government networks for quantum-era threats while supporting long-term modernization.
Today, Elisity IdentityGraph combines native asset identity and partner-enriched context, and risk information to inform least-privilege access policy for users, devices, workloads and AI agents. Teams can simulate policies before limiting each identity to the communications it needs, helping reduce attack surface and contain an attack’s spread. By bringing together Elisity's Zero Trust framework with IonQ's PQC and QKD capabilities, the companies will combine cryptographic protection for sensitive information and communications with identity-based controls that limit unauthorized access and the spread of threats across enterprise networks. The shared roadmap with IonQ will extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information. This integrated approach will help customers address quantum-related security risks through a multiyear transition while strengthening defenses against current cyberattacks, including threats involving AI agents.
Following closing, Elisity will continue serving its customers under its current leadership, including current CEO James Winebrenner. Together, the companies will continue their track record of innovation, customer success and strong partner relationships, backed by IonQ’s demonstrated approach of investing in the critical technologies it acquires.
IonQ’s Multiproduct Revenue Growth Opportunity
IonQ brings an established track record in growing its quantum security and quantum-secure communications offering. The company has deployed some of the largest quantum-safe national communications networks in the world, including in Switzerland, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and serves global customers with quantum-safe defense in depth spanning quantum-safe posture management, quantum key distribution, and post quantum cryptography.
Customers are increasingly adopting multiple IonQ products and services, driving growth in multiproduct revenue and providing evidence of demand for integrated solutions; in the second quarter of 2026, IonQ delivered 40% year-over-year growth in multiproduct revenue..
IonQ and Elisity expect opportunities to cross-sell complementary security solutions, expand relationships with enterprise and government customers, and develop integrated offerings.
Under the terms of the agreement, IonQ will acquire Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in earnout opportunity subject to performance of the Elisity business. The number of IonQ shares to be issued in the transaction will be calculated at closing based on the volume weighted average price of IonQ common stock for the 20 trading days prior to, but not including, the third business day before the closing date, but that price will not be greater than $49.61 or less than $33.07 per share.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approval.
Elisity helps enterprises advance Zero Trust security for users, devices, workloads, AI agents and other non-human identities. Elisity IdentityGraph correlates identity, asset and risk information from native and partner sources to inform access decisions. Elisity’s software policy layer uses the network to enforce access rules independently of the underlying network technology. Teams can simulate policies and limit each identity to the communications it needs, extending the value of existing network and security investments. Founded in 2019, Elisity has a global employee footprint and a growing number of customers in the Fortune 500. Learn more at elisity.com .
IonQ, Inc . [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the Superion, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance .
Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations across North America, Latin America, EMEA, and APAC. Our quantum computing services have been available through all major cloud providers since 2021, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com .

articles.title_orig: A multidisciplinary research institute to guide the business world
articles.title_zh: A multidisciplinary research institute to guide the business world
articles.content_orig:
Housed within the Fox School of Business, Temple’s Responsible Business Institute (RBI) is a new multidisciplinary hub for research, dialogue and innovation that has launched this fall.
Housed in the Fox School of Business, the Responsible Business Institute is directed by Leora Eisenstadt and serves as a multidisciplinary hub for research, dialogue and innovation.
Photo by Ryan S. Brandenberg
Only 53% of Americans believe large U.S. companies are very or somewhat just , the lowest percentage that the number has been since it started being tracked by JUST Capital seven years ago. That same study also indicates that 80% percent of Americans think that business still can be a force for positive change. For today’s business leaders, this presents a challenge. The public wants to see companies and organizations do well, but there is a general disbelief in their ability to do so. So, how can leaders be provided with the necessary tools to create highly efficient workforces that thrive within productive, innovative and inclusive workplace cultures? That is where the Responsible Business Institute (RBI) comes in. Housed within Temple University’s Fox School of Business, RBI is a new multidisciplinary hub for research, dialogue and innovation that has launched this fall. “The idea of the Responsible Business Institute is to focus on the pillars that every responsible business should be focused on and viewing those pillars as interrelated. So, ethics and compliance; sustainability, inclusion and workplace culture. The key is not viewing each of those in a vacuum but viewing them as connected in the way that a company strategizes and moves forward. That is the starting point for how we hope to educate business leaders moving forward,” said Leora Eisenstadt, RBI’s director who is also an associate professor in the Department of Risk, Actuarial Science, Healthcare Management and Legal Studies at the Fox School. The institute represents the evolution of the Center for Ethics, Diversity and Workplace Culture (CEDWC), which previously operated out of Fox. RBI reflects a broader and more interdisciplinary vision for the future of organizational leadership and impact, and that can be seen through its various partners across campus. While the institute is housed in Fox, it is a universitywide institute supported by Temple’s Office of the Vice President for Research. “The Fox School is excited to host this new institute and join our campus partners in fostering more of the world-class research that Temple University is known for, as well as finding applications of that research in dialogue with our corporate partners and the broader community,” said Chip Hunter, dean of Fox and the School of Sport, Tourism and Hospitality Management. “This cross-campus collaboration reinforces the strategic commitment made by the university to realizing sustainable, positive impact in Greater Philadelphia and beyond.” “RBI embodies research in action, bringing researchers and corporate and community partners together to address the challenges organizations face,” added Josh Gladden, Temple’s vice president for research. “By translating evidence into practical tools, RBI will help our partners develop a skilled, adaptable workforce, strengthen business competitiveness and support economic growth while creating the conditions for people to thrive. This is what drives research at Temple: advancing knowledge that makes a meaningful difference in people's lives and in communities.” The initiative is also supported by five additional Temple schools and colleges, including the College of Public Health; the Beasley School of Law; the College of Liberal Arts; the Klein College of Media and Communication; and the School of Sport, Tourism and Hospitality Management. Each school has an RBI fellow, who works in tandem with Eisenstadt on RBI’s various initiatives and research. “Each of the fellows has a different sort of research focus, but they’re all interested in translational research. So, the idea is the same idea we had with CEDWC, in that we are focusing on research sponsorship, educational programming and industry engagement. But now, we are approaching this work from so many more disciplines. That is exciting because it means our impact will grow,” Eisenstadt said. "For me, it’s been great to see the institute’s commitment to fostering an interdisciplinary community. I’ve had two opportunities to present my research regarding disability,” said Dustin Kidd, professor of sociology in the College of Liberal Arts and a faculty fellow at RBI. Kidd used the faculty fellowship to make progress on a forthcoming book. The ultimate goal with RBI’s expanded approach is for the institute to engage more deeply with complex organizational issues influencing the future of work and responsible business leadership. This is intended to be across industries, as well. So, for instance, RBI may partner with a large corporation on one research project but the institute is just as likely to work with a smaller nonprofit organization on another. “When you're thinking about how to handle whistleblowing policy in your company, you shouldn’t be doing that in a vacuum, and you probably shouldn’t have to pay consulting companies hundreds of thousands of dollars if you’re a corporate partner with an academic institution that is doing leading research on this. You should look to us,” Eisenstadt said. “So, one of the things we’re doing is saying to our faculty fellows, when you publish new research, we want you to then go to our corporate partners and say, in layman’s terms, here’s what my research means to you.” Helping guide the institute as it pursues its new work is a highly qualified, senior advisory board led by Board Chair Timothy Fair, vice president of culture and community impact at Burlington Stores Inc. The board also includes representation from companies and organizations that include EY, Nixon Peabody LLP, Lincoln Financial, PwC and Merrill Lynch. RBI will formally launch later this fall when the institute hosts a special panel event, titled “Ethical AI? Can AI be deployed responsibly across people, processes and the planet?” Scheduled for Monday, Oct. 26, from 12:30 to 2 p.m. in Alter Hall, the event will feature an insightful and engaging conversation with industry leaders from Intel, Google DeepMind and Nike.
