articles.title_orig: Robert E. Hall wins Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
articles.title_zh: Robert E. Hall wins Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.
The illustrations are free to use for non-commercial purposes. Attribute ”© Johan Jarnestad/The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences”

Robert E. Hall , born 1943 in Palo Alto, CA, USA. PhD 1967 from Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA. Professor at Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford , born 1955 in Chicopee, MA, USA. PhD 1983 from Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, USA. Professor at Columbia University, New York, USA.
Prize amount : 12 million Swedish kronor, to be shared equally between the laureates. Further information : www.kva.se and www.nobelprize.org Press contact : Eva Nevelius, Press Secretary, +46 70 878 67 63, [email protected] Experts : Timo Boppart, +41-774 84 30 00, [email protected] , John Hassler, +46 70-811 72 63, [email protected] , Per Krusell, +46 70-276 13 34, [email protected] , members of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, founded in 1739, is an independent organisation whose overall objective is to promote the sciences and strengthen their influence in society. The Academy takes special responsibility for the natural sciences and mathematics, but endeavours to promote the exchange of ideas between various disciplines.
Nobel Prize® is a registered trademark of the Nobel Foundation.
Six prizes were awarded for achievements that have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind. The 10 laureates' work and discoveries range from optogenetics to efforts to promote peace and international law.

articles.title_orig: Delta delays debut of Saudi Arabia service until March after Riyadh airport attacks
articles.title_zh: Delta delays debut of Saudi Arabia service until March after Riyadh airport attacks
articles.content_orig:
Delta Air Lines said it will delay the launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and the Saudi capital Riyadh until March after several deadly attacks hit the city's airport there.
Delta planned to begin the route on Oct. 23, with an Airbus A350-900 wide-body plane, in what would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia operated by a U.S. airline.
Since Thursday, more than 2,000 flights have been canceled to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to FlightAware. The deadly attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.
King Khalid International Airport remains closed as of Monday.
"We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation," Delta said in a statement. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term."
Delta CEO Ed Bastian had told CNBC on Thursday that the airline hadn't yet decided whether to postpone the debut.
"Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," he said. "Safety is going to make the call."
Delta's decision came after the Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday issued a warning for U.S. airlines.
The FAA said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. In the warning, which is in effect until Dec. 10, the agency said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes."
Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week, while countries including the U.S. and Australia advised citizens against travel to the region.
— CNBC's Michele Luhn contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.title_zh: Saudi minister vows 'serious response' to Houthi attacks on airports
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister has vowed a "serious" response to the deadly attacks on the kingdom's airports and oil and gas facilities by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement.
"The events of recent weeks are serious. Our response must be equally serious," Prince Abdul Aziz bin Salman told the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh.
On Sunday, a Pakistani man was killed in an attack on a terminal at the capital's King Khalid International Airport, Saudi authorities said. It came a day after a Houthi missile hit another terminal, killing 13 people and forcing its closure.
The Houthis said they launched the attacks in retaliation for "brutal Saudi aggression" against areas they control in western Yemen.
The Houthi-run health ministry said a child was killed and six other people were injured in a Saudi air strike on a home in the capital, Sanaa, on Sunday.
A Saudi-led coalition is providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces battling the Houthis on Yemen's Red Sea coast and other areas.
The WPC Energy Congress opened on Sunday at a convention centre about 10km (6 miles) from Riyadh's airport, which has been attacked four times over the past week.
Last Thursday, three Saudis, including a pilot for the national airline Saudia, were killed in two strikes on an airport facility and an aircraft on the ground.
Another four Saudis, as well as two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian, one Sudanese and one Indian, were killed in Saturday's missile strike on Terminal 3.
On Sunday, a Pakistani resident was killed when a projectile hit Terminal 4, according to the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).
King Fahd International Airport in the north-eastern city of Dammam was also attacked on Sunday evening, it said, but no casualties were reported.
Later, the Saudi-led coalition said its forces had intercepted a drone in Eastern Province and a missile launched by the Houthis towards the south-western city of Khamis Mushait.
In his inaugural address to the WPC Energy Congress on Monday, Prince Abdul Aziz thanked industry executives and policymakers for attending despite the attacks.
"You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart," he said.
But he also acknowledged that "energy security cannot be taken for granted" and that recent developments had "tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience".
Prince Abdul Aziz promised that his country would overcome those challenges.
"We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people," he said. "We shall prove it to the world that whatever we are going through we will overcome it."
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.
On Sunday evening, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said in a video statement that its forces had launched missiles and drones at Riyadh and Dammam's airports, as well as two oil and gas facilities in Eastern Province, in response to 124 Saudi air strikes in Yemen over the previous 24 hours.
Sarea also reiterated a warning to airlines and passengers against using Saudi airports and airspace, except for journeys to and from the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina.
The Houthis' forces, he vowed, would "continue their escalating operations deep inside Saudi, imposing the equation of 'a blockade for a blockade' and 'an escalation for an escalation' and targeting Saudi enemy reinforcements until the aggression ceases and the siege on our dear people is lifted".
Saturday's attack on Riyadh airport drew widespread international condemnation.
UN Secretary General António Guterres said he was "deeply shocked" and warned that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure were a violation of international law.
President Donald Trump said he would "make a decision" about the US joining Saudi Arabia's strikes on the Houthis. The US military is reportedly already providing intelligence and targeting support to the Saudi-led coalition.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied allegations that it provides weapons and training to the Houthis, said it was "deeply concerned" by the escalation and called for "dialogue and engagement" to resolve the situation.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The Yemeni government claimed it was behind that strike, saying it was trying to prevent an unauthorised Iranian plane from landing.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports after the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
Last week, the Yemeni government announced the start of a new offensive aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Pro-government forces said they were quickly able to retake areas around Bab al-Mandab with the help of intense Saudi air strikes, but the Houthis denied losing any territory.

articles.title_orig: Alexander Zverev to end year as world number one after Carlos Alcaraz loses
articles.title_zh: Alexander Zverev to end year as world number one after Carlos Alcaraz loses
articles.content_orig:
Alexander Zverev will be the 30th man to be ranked number one on the ATP Tour
Alexander Zverev is guaranteed to finish the 2026 season as world number one after Carlos Alcaraz's surprise defeat in the Shanghai Masters.
German Zverev was on course to climb above current world number one Jannik Sinner, who has been ruled out for the rest of the year with a knee injury.
Alcaraz still had a mathematical chance of stopping Zverev until he was beaten 7-5 7-6 (7-4) by Belgium's Zizou Bergs in the third round on Monday.
"It's been a fantastic season for me. Knowing that I will finish the year on top of the rankings is just a dream come true," said Zverev.
After losing three major finals, Zverev landed the first Grand Slam title of his career by winning the French Open in June, and followed that with victory at the US Open last month.
The 29-year-old has taken advantage of the injury problems suffered by Spaniard Alcaraz and Italian Sinner - the dominant pair on the ATP Tour in the previous two seasons - to become the world's leading player.
Zverev cannot overtake Sinner until 2 November at the earliest.
He will become the first German man to end the year as number one, and the oldest player to achieve the feat for the first time.
After suffering a serious ankle injury in the 2022 French Open semi-finals which kept him out for seven months, Zverev regained his place in the upper echelons of the sport and been ranked inside the top four continuously since March 2024.
"So much work and effort have been put into achieving this goal, especially after coming back from the ankle injury. I look forward to finishing the season in style," he added.
At the start of the year it seemed unthinkable that anybody other than Sinner or Alcaraz would finish it as world number one.
Going into 2026, Alcaraz led the rankings with 12,050 points, closely followed by Sinner on 11,500.
The dominance of the pair - who split all of the eight Grand Slam titles in 2024 and 2025 between them - was illustrated by the huge gap to the rest of the field.
Third-ranked Zverev had 5,110 points - closer numerically to the 2,221st player in the rankings than the top two.
But as the season enters its final stretch, Zverev has completed what many thought was impossible.
There is no escaping the fact that Zverev has benefitted from Sinner and Alcaraz missing large chunks of the season through injury, meaning he won the French Open and US Open titles with at least one of the pair absent.
Both his major wins came without having to face Sinner or Alcaraz, and he did not face a top-10 player until beating Ben Shelton in the New York final.
Zverev has said he would "maybe not" be the world's best player if both his rivals were "healthy and at the top of their game".
But, as the old adage goes, you can only beat what is in front of you.
Zverev has done exactly that to record the greatest season of a career which had threatened to fall short of the lofty expectations placed on him since he emerged as a teenage prodigy.
Alcaraz has made encouraging progress since returning from a wrist injury which kept him off tour for almost five months, but this was a reminder that coming back from such a long absence is not smooth sailing.
The seven-time Grand Slam champion was below the level he showed in winning the Japan Open last week as he produced a string of uncharacteristic errors.
"Today wasn't a good match from my side. I didn't feel good," said Alcaraz, who also credited 39th-ranked Bergs for serving strongly and taking his chances.
"Right now, all the negative thoughts come to my mind and none of the positives, but I think [later] I will take the good things."
Bergs, who showed great composure to serve out the biggest win of his career, faces American Tommy Paul in the last 16.
Zverev remains in the draw as one of only three top-eight seeds left, alongside Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime and Russia's Daniil Medvedev.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction in Southeast: "Never expected to be 77 years old and go through this"
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction in Southeast: "Never expected to be 77 years old and go through this"
articles.content_orig:
Hurricane Isaias left behind a trail of destruction from Florida's Gulf Coast to the Carolinas over the weekend after slamming onto shore near Destin, Florida, as a Category 2 storm.
The storm made landfall on Friday night and roared through the Southeast. At least two people were killed in Florida and two were killed in Alabama.
Some of the most violent wind gusts from the hurricane were recorded 15 miles away from the coast, in Milton, Florida. The wind there took down a massive tree, which fell on top of a house. Phyllis Hennebery said she was in her room lying down when the tree fell.
"I never expected to be 77 years old and go through this," she said, showing CBS News destruction from the fallen tree in the ceiling above her.
The hurricane shredded roofs off apartments and tore away walls that once enclosed bedrooms. On Monday morning, more than 150,000 customers in Florida were still without power, according to poweroutage.us . More than 20,000 others were without power in Alabama.
Pastor Jonathan Kaushal's church group was handing out food and water after the storm.
"Lots of people in need after the hurricane and so we just want to be there for the community," he said.
The remnants of the storm also spun off at least eight confirmed tornadoes in Georgia and the Carolinas, including one that ripped off the roof of a home about 90 miles west of Charleston.
In western North Carolina, more than half a foot of rain flooded roads.
As Isaias moved through the Southeast, the West Coast was feeling the impact of another significant storm. What's left of Tropical Storm Rachel sent massive 8-foot waves pounding beachfront homes south of Los Angeles.
The Coast Guard rescued a man by helicopter who was trapped in a sailboat that ran onshore Sunday morning.
Flooding also spread into southern Nevada, swamping the Las Vegas Strip.
Severe weather also slammed Utah during the Moab 240, a five-day-long ultramarathon. Around 70 runners were rescued by bus after they were stranded by dangerous floods.

articles.title_orig: First Impressions: Dell XPS Googlebook and the Googlebook OS
articles.title_zh: First Impressions: Dell XPS Googlebook and the Googlebook OS
articles.content_orig:
Posted on October 12, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 10 Comments
As someone who has, over the years, found himself deep in the Google ecosystem of hardware and services, I had been curious about the Googlebook concept for a while — whether it would be basically a fancy Chromebook, or if it would offer something more, and more useful , than that line of affordable but mostly limited laptops. When the Googlebook models were announced in September, I decided to go ahead and pre-order one: The Acer Googlebook 14.
It turns out, however, that apparently lots of people had the same idea as me. Best Buy sent me an email telling me that despite taking my pre-order money, the Acer was out of stock and they didn’t know when they would get more. I cancelled that order and went with the Dell XPS Googlebook instead, which, I think by virtue of being $100 more expensive than the Acer, was in stock. It arrived the day after I ordered it — and when, alas, I was away at New York Comic Con for a few days. I finally got a chance to set it up and play with it yesterday.
My first impressions: It’s pretty nice! Also, Google still has work to do on its shiny new operating system.
Hardware first: The XPS Googlebook is a really nice little laptop. It’s physically the smallest of the five Googlebooks available at launch (the other four coming from Acer, Asus, Hewlett-Packard and Lenovo). It’s clearly meant to be in the “ultrabook” category of laptop, which is to say, light and thin and not terribly concerned with ports (it comes with two USB-C ports and that’s it — not even a headphone jack). It’s also the only Googlebook at launch that does not come with an OLED screen, although the screen it has is perfectly nice and the blacks are certainly inky enough for government work.
All of the launch Googlebooks were required by Google to have certain minimum hardware: at least 16GB of RAM, high-speed processors, either by Intel or Qualcomm (the XPS comes with a Snapdragon X Elite), 512GB SSD, a metal, not plastic, chassis, backlit keyboard, and a touchscreen with a high refresh rate (120 Hz here). None of this comes cheap these days, and the initial set of Googlebooks are priced between $899 and $1299, with the XPS I got coming in at $999. This is more expensive than just about any Chromebook, more expensive than the new Macbook Neo, and on par with a newish Macbook Air.
The minimum requirements pay off, at least for the XPS. It feels really solid for such a small computer, and everything about it looks and feels nice. The keyboard has a nice snap to it and has almost no flex, the screen as mentioned is very good (and comes with an anti-glare coating, which is a feature I appreciate now that I have it), and while it has fans, which turned on while I was setting up the laptop, they are quiet and barely noticeable when they’re on, which so far has only been during that setup.
As mentioned the processor here is a Snapdragon chip rather than an Intel one, and that’s fine because Android (which the Googlebook OS is based on, and which, frankly, it’s mostly just a reskinned version of) is designed to run on ARM chips, which Snapdragon is. Everything runs quickly so far, and ARM chips are typically meant to be more efficient than x86 chips like Intel’s, although so far the battery life I’ve seen out of the XPS is good but not amazing.
The XPS has quirks — the keyboard is a modified Chromebook set-up, which means the Caps button is a “search” button first (you can make it a Caps button by holding down the shift button, which defeats the whole purpose of a caps button), and there’s a “Google” button on the bottom row which opens an app drawer or can be used to access the “magic pointer” (more on that later). Also, the speakers, while perfectly acceptable, make the chassis vibrate, particularly the trackpad, which is a not entirely pleasant feeling. The trackpad is mechanical, not haptic, and the click does take some pressure (it responds to taps perfectly well). The I/O situation as mentioned is sparse, but inasmuch as I already have a MacBook Air, which also only has two USB-C ports, I am already well-acquainted with the dongle life, and I have bluetooth headphones. I’m not going to give the XPS too much crap for that.
So as a piece of hardware, the XPS is solid. Now, how is the software — the Googlebook operating system and all the “AI” bells and whistles that Google has piled on top of it?
As a preface, I should note that I knew going into this that as an early adopter of this platform, I would essentially be a beta tester for it, since almost no 1.0 release of anything survives its first encounter with users out in the world. In the week since Googlebooks have hit the market there have already been updates to the OS to fix bugs and other flubs. So I’m okay with having a little patience in this shake-down cruise. That said, being patient doesn’t mean not pointing out the flaws that do currently exist.
One of those flaws is that at the moment the Googlebook is doing a crap job at one of its marquee features, namely, integration with Android phones, where one is supposed to be able to connect laptop and phone seamlessly, stream apps from the phone to the laptop, hand off work from one to the other, and drop files from one into the other painlessly. As a Pixel phone owner, this promised integration was a huge inducement to try out the Googlebook — I wanted what (presumably) iPhone users have with their Macs. It would, in fact, be really useful. And as a Pixel owner running Android 17, I am someone best positioned to get that integration right out of the box.
Except that the Googlebook keeps dropping its connection to my phone and not being able to find it after that, unless I restart both the phone and the Googlebook. It happens when I take my phone away from the laptop and/or close the laptop, breaking the connection between the two. A short disconnect doesn’t seem to be a problem; a longer one seems to flummox it entirely. I believe this is a known issue that’s being addressed, so that’s good. But it’s still annoying right now . I don’t want to have to keep resetting my laptop and phone to get the promised integration.
(I’ve also noticed that phone apps streamed onto the Googlebook can have choppy scrolling, although I don’t know if that’s a problem with the integration or an artifact of my occasionally-janky internet connection.)
That said, when the integration does work, it’s pretty neat, and I see it being really useful when I’m working on my laptop and need something from my phone, or want to access an app that I don’t have running natively on my computer. As mentioned already, the Googlebook OS is pretty much a reskinned version of Android 17, so all the apps that run on an Android phone should run just fine on the laptop (there are apps that apparently struggle on the Intel Googlebooks, but even there something like 97% of apps run perfectly well). During the setup, if you pair your Googlebook with your phone it will install the apps you have there over to the laptop, so you’ll be able to run them natively even if you can’t access your phone. But they are different instances of the app, so streaming an app might still come in handy.
So: Great in concept! Execution still needs work.
Google is going all in on “AI” integration on the Googlebooks, making sure that Gemini, its in-house “AI,” is only a click, button-mash or cursor wiggle away, the latter being the “magic pointer” feature. You can invoke Gemini and ask it about what’s on your screen, or have it smoosh two images you have into a single “AI”-ified picture and so on (the Googlebooks also come with an offer for an entire year of the “Pro” level of Gemini, which comes with five terabytes of cloud storage, which is arguably more useful). The point is, no matter where you go on the Googlebook OS, Gemini is right there, lurking, waiting for you to do something with it.

articles.title_orig: California used to play the world. Now, ‘East of Eden’ gets shot in New Zealand
articles.title_zh: California used to play the world. Now, ‘East of Eden’ gets shot in New Zealand
articles.content_orig:
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
We all know how much Hollywood film production has been battered in the last few years. Yet my heart still sank a bit when I learned the highly anticipated Netflix miniseries of John Steinbeck’s “East of Eden” — one of the great California epics — was filmed on location in New Zealand.
It’s a minor indignity in the scheme of things, though it did remind me of the days when it seemed every TV show, movie, music video and commercial was shot in California. Los Angeles led the way as a stand-in for everything and everywhere.

As a latchkey kid who watched hour after hour of television in the afternoons, I took pride in spotting my city despite the camouflage. The errant palm tree in the English countryside manor. The quintessentially black L.A. traffic lights and blue signage in a bustling “Manhattan streetscape.” The distant San Gabriel Mountains behind what was supposed to be a Midwestern city.
The magic act was part Hollywood craftsmanship, part perfect location. Back then, it was smoggy so much of the year that the cityscape seemed to fade away after a few blocks into a gray screen, creating a pollution-fueled soundstage.
Today, Los Angeles struggles as productions flee to places including New Jersey, Georgia, London and Albuquerque, which are taking their turns as urban shape-shifters. But it was L.A. that pioneered it.
The promise of year-round filming is one reason the entertainment industry moved to Hollywood in the first place. There is that famous 1927 Paramount Pictures map of California suggesting how different locales could be used for filming: Palos Verdes as Wales, Santa Barbara as the Spanish Riviera, the Mojave as the Sahara, the Sierra as Switzerland.
The downtown Los Angeles of the 1970s, ’80s and ’90s really felt like a back lot. The city center was famously run down, vacant and filled with neglected architectural gems perfect for any project. The Times chronicled the intense competition for downtown filming space in a story titled “We’ll Fake Manhattan.”
“It serves for just about anyplace, USA,” a location scout said in 1998. “A great deal of downtown L.A. not only looks like New York but other major cities.”
During those boom days, productions were lining up to take over the prime spots. Spring Street for the Art Deco  look. Broadway for its movie palaces and Manhattan street scene. Certain alleyways were favored for chases and gangster murders. Figueroa or Flower streets for the corporate look. What is now the Arts District for industrial grit.
Downtown was still hot a decade ago when I wandered out of The Times’ old newsroom to see the side of City Hall transformed into Washington, D.C. A few blocks away on Spring Street, a real-life-scale Manhattan subway station emerged (on closer examination, the staircase down ended after two steps).
Downtown Los Angeles is still a hub for filming, but it’s just not the same. As my colleagues Samantha Masunaga and Stacy Perman reported, film shoot days in L.A. have fallen nearly 50% since 2019, while the motion picture industry has shed around 57,000 jobs in four years. Increasingly, we hear about places such as Atlanta and Vancouver filling in for Los Angeles. (Don’t get me  started about HBO shooting a 2011 miniseries version of the L.A. crime classic “Mildred Pierce” in Long Island!)
In 2003, filmmaker Thom Andersen produced an influential and highly entertaining documentary about how film portrays the city called “Los Angeles Plays Itself.”
I’d love a companion film called “Los Angeles Plays Someone Else.”
It could include some of my favorites, starting with the unassuming apartment building on New Hampshire Avenue in Koreatown that became the home of the ultimate Manhattanite: Jerry Seinfeld.
And it would end with “Friends With Benefits,”  starring Justin Timberlake and Mila Kunis.
The 2011 romantic comedy intentionally mocks L.A. as a location for so many New York movies. Dylan (Justin) and Jamie (Mila) are getting cozy watching a faux New York rom-com on TV. It’s clearly filmed at L.A.’s Union Station as a highly unrealistic fill-in for Grand Central Station.  Dylan calls it out, just as the couple on screen embark on a Central Park horse-drawn carriage through a sea of L.A. palm trees.
So now, New Zealand has its chance to play California. Steinbeck’s book takes place in the late 19th and early 20th  centuries in Salinas and Monterey. Portions of the 1955 Elia Kazan movie were shot in Salinas and along the Mendocino Coast. The director of the new miniseries, Zoe Kazan, made a fair point about picking New Zealand, telling Netflix that “there’s a lot of unspoiled landscape in a way that would be much harder to find here. The actual Salinas Valley doesn’t look the way that it did anymore.”
It turns out her grandfather felt the same way. Elia Kazan believed the Salinas of the 1950s was way too modern for many key scenes, according to a detailed story of the production in American Cinematographer that originally ran in the publication in 1955. So he filmed a good deal back at the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank, painstakingly re-creating Salinas down to the detailed carvings of the wood and the products on the store shelves. “The Research department heads spent several weeks in Salinas gathering old photographs and information from the citizenry about the town as it was prior to our entry into World War I,” the article said.
And Salinas didn’t seem to mind. When the movie came out, Steinbeck himself penned a piece for the Salinas Californian, declaring it “probably the best movie I’ve ever seen.”
‘I’m not gonna sit in a corner and cry for him when I have so much to do,’ Blanca Ortiz says. ‘I need to figure out how to pay the mortgage, how to pay the bills, how to keep the shop running.’
More adorable than spooky, these Halloween treats are nothing more than homemade marshmallows , using just a handful of ingredients. Although the recipe does require the use of a candy thermometer, the hardest part is probably piping the “ghost” shapes just right.
What is your favorite Halloween candy?
Jody S. says, “I’ll shamelessly admit this. The most maligned Halloween candy out there is my all-time favorite: candy corn!”
Glenn C. says, “Nestle Crunch are my favorite Halloween candy.”

articles.title_orig: World, religious leaders unite in prayer for Pope Leo, praising his ‘profound serenity and transparency’
articles.title_zh: World, religious leaders unite in prayer for Pope Leo, praising his ‘profound serenity and transparency’
articles.content_orig:
(OSV News) — Prominent political and religious leaders from around the world expressed well wishes and prayers for Pope Leo XIV after he announced he would undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule.
The pope made the surprise announcement while addressing pilgrims Oct. 11 during his Sunday Angelus address.
After doctors detected “a small, localized nodule” in his lung, Pope Leo said he would follow their advice and “undergo surgery to remove it.”
“The operation is already scheduled to take place in the coming days,” he said. ” I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers.”
Not long after his announcement, Italian President Sergio Mattarella published a letter to Pope Leo saying that the news of his surgery “was received with deep empathy and emotion by all the Italian people.”
“In view of your hospitalization in the coming days, may the affectionate thoughts of all Italians reach you, which I convey while adding my own personal sentiments,” Mattarella wrote. “The Italian people stand close to you.”
The Italian head of state said the pope could count on the prayers of not only the Catholic faithful, but also “on the caring thoughts of countless people, in Italy as well as across the world, whether believers or non-believers.”
Several world leaders also took to X to send well wishes to the pope, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who wished Pope Leo “a successful surgery and a swift, full recovery.”
“Our thoughts and prayers are with him, and we hope he will soon be back in good health and strength,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Ukraine is deeply grateful to His Holiness for his prayers and his strong, consistent calls for a dignified and durable peace.”
In a brief message posted to X, Israeli President Isaac Herzog wrote: “From the holy city of Jerusalem, I wish Pope Leo XIV a full and speedy recovery.”
Maltese Prime Minister Robert Abela also extended “prayers and best wishes” to the pope for “a successful procedure and a complete recovery.”
Pope Leo also received prayers from Anglican Archbishop Sarah Mullaly of Canterbury, who said she was “holding Pope Leo XIV in my prayers over these coming days, asking for God’s protection, closeness and care.”
“With Christians across the country and around the world, I pray for the pope’s swift recovery,” the head of the Church of England wrote on X.
Viktor Eichner, the World Jewish Congress’ representative to the Holy See, also posted on X, writing: “On behalf of the World Jewish Congress, I wish Pope Leo XIV a successful surgery and a speedy recovery. May he return to full strength soon.”
The surgery announcement came as Pope Leo prepares to embark on his longest international trip to date: a 12-day apostolic visit to Latin America, including stops in Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.
At the Angelus, the pope greeted a group of Peruvian pilgrims and thanked them for praying for his upcoming visit, indicating the trip was still moving forward.
At a press conference in Uruguay, the first stop in the pope’s Nov. 6-17 apostolic trip, Cardinal Daniel Sturla of Montevideo told journalists Oct. 11 that although the announcement “was a surprise,” the pope’s greetings to the Peruvian pilgrims showed that “the plans remain the same.”
“Obviously, we are all praying for the pope’s health and trust that everything will go well, that he will recover and be able to be here on the scheduled date,” Cardinal Sturla said.
When asked if any precautions will be taken given that the pope is expected to arrive in less than a month, the Uruguayan cardinal said he believed so and that the pope “always travels accompanied by his personal physician and other healthcare staff.”
“I understand that some care will need to be taken,” Cardinal Sturla said. “We will be instructed in the coming days. We will be very attentive to that, but confident that everything will go well and that we are moving forward.”
Argentine President Javier Milei extended his “affection and best wishes” ahead of the pope’s surgery. Pope Leo will visit Argentina Nov. 8-11.
“All of Argentina accompanies His Holiness with affection and prayer, wishing him a prompt and full recovery,” Milei wrote on X. “From our country, we join in prayer for his health, in the hope that he may soon continue guiding the Church with his characteristic wisdom and strength.”
The Argentine bishops’ conference issued a statement calling on the country’s Catholics to pray for Pope Leo ahead of his surgery.
“We ask the Lord to grant him strength and peace at this time, that the surgery proceeds favorably, and that he may achieve a prompt and full recovery,” the bishops wrote.
Noting the pope’s “serenity and confidence” in his announcement, the bishops urged Catholics to “remain spiritually united with him.”
In Peru, where Pope Leo is scheduled to visit Nov. 11-17, President Keiko Fujimori took to X to express her and her country’s “profound affection and solidarity” with the pope “in the face of this health issue, which we hope he will overcome fully and successfully.”
“Our hearts and our prayers are with him, in the hope of soon having him among us,” Fujimori wrote. “With deep faith and hope, we pray that the Holy Father has a prompt recovery and may continue guiding, with wisdom and strength, the path of faith of the entire Holy Church.”
In a statement released shortly after the pope’s announcement, Bishop Carlos Enrique García Camader of Lurin, president of the Peruvian bishops’ conference, noted the pope’s “profound serenity and transparency” in announcing his surgery and that his “testimony of fortitude and humility in sharing this news moves us and immediately calls us to unity in prayer.”
“The Peruvian Episcopate invites all Catholic people and people of goodwill to unite in prayer for the health of His Holiness Pope Leo XIV, raising our supplications to God, Lord of life and source of all health, so that He may strengthen him and grant him the health required for the fulfillment of his mission,” Bishop García wrote.
He also invoked Mary’s intercession “so that in the fullness of his strength he may continue fulfilling his mission in service to the Church and all humanity, continuing to be a messenger of peace and hope, and a witness of unity, fraternity, and encounter among all peoples.”
Junno Arocho Esteves is an international correspondent for OSV News. Follow him on X @jae_journalist

articles.title_orig: Trump expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
articles.title_zh: Trump expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
articles.content_orig:
Washington — A growing number of Republicans are voicing concern over the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood shooter in December — or at the very least, saying they won't be watching.
Over the weekend, President Trump said the administration was still making a determination about whether the firing-squad execution would be livestreamed, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that it would be. The execution of Nidal Hasan , the ex-Army major convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, is scheduled for Dec. 3.
House Speaker Mike Johnson told CBS News that some in the House Republican conference don't approve, and said he planned on bringing those concerns to the White House.
"There are colleagues who have concerns," Johnson told national correspondent and chief Washington analyst Robert Costa in an interview . "The concern would be that you would create a video that would be a recruiting tool for future terrorists. You know, we've got to think through the policy implications of all that. I wouldn't be watching it if it was aired. But there's a lot of opinions on that. I think there's still some time to talk about that. ... I need to tell the White House what some of my colleagues think about that, and not everybody is in favor of the idea."
Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one," urging the Pentagon to change course.
"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," she wrote on X . "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks. How we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself, so I urge the Pentagon to reverse this gruesome decision."
Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said in a statement, "The death penalty is not entertainment." He said families of the victims deserve justice. "But publicizing the execution of religious extremists provides exactly what terrorists crave: an audience. It converts the most consequential punishment a government can impose into a public spectacle."
"Justice will be served, but the United States of America does not and should not livestream executions," Republican Rep. Ann Wagner of Missouri wrote on X.
Rep. Rob Bresnahan Jr. of Pennsylvania wrote , "An execution shouldn't be a live-streamed spectacle. The focus should be on justice for the victims and their families, not turning an execution into entertainment. Their pain deserves respect, not a public show."
Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina on Friday called livestreaming the execution "beyond disgusting."
Only one Republican member of Congress has publicly voiced clear support for livestreaming the execution — Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee.: "Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves," he wrote on X . "We will be watching."
Vice President JD Vance said Friday that he wouldn't be watching if it's livestreamed, and added, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance told reporters. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the livestreaming decision on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" this weekend. Asked if the administration risks making Hasan a martyr, Mullin responded, "No one has to watch it." Pressed further on whether the decision risks radicalizing others, Mullin said, "I think people need to understand if you attack— if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the— that the punishment fits the crime."
On Saturday, Mr. Trump floated the possibility that the plans could still change.
"There are two thoughts: don't show it and show it," the president told reporters at the White House Saturday. "'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I'll make a decision."
The president has given seemingly conflicting information as to whether he was involved in the decision to livestream the execution.
When a reporter asked the president Friday if he authorized or approved the livestreaming decision, he said, "Absolutely, I did." But in an interview with CNY Central Syracuse later that day, he said he "wasn't involved in that decision" to livestream the execution, while saying he understood that decision was made to "have it serve as an example."

articles.title_orig: At least 20 injured in northern Israel explosion
articles.title_zh: At least 20 injured in northern Israel explosion
articles.content_orig:
One person has been killed and 19 others were injured in an explosion in northern Israel near the Lebanese border, according to preliminary official tallies, in an incident that is under investigation.
“I share in the heavy grief of the family of the boy who was killed in the explosion during the trip near the northern border, and I wish a swift and full recovery to all the injured,” Israel’s Defence Minister Israel Katz posted on X, adding that authorities were looking into the cause of the blast.
Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the victim was a 15-year-old who had gone on an annual school trip.
Citing medical sources, the Israeli police earlier said that “the initial suspicion is that it was caused by an unexploded ordnance, as a result of which about 20 people were injured with varying degrees of severity.” The explosion occurred near the community of Neot Mordechai, between Kibbutz Manara and Kibbutz Yiftach.
The incident injured both students and staff from a religious high school as they were on an outing, the municipality of the northern city of Maalot-Tarshiha said.
There is a heavy military deployment in the north of the country and in parts of southern Lebanon as Israel continues attacks it says target the Iran-aligned Hezbollah group.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank said that some of the injured are described to be in critical condition.
“There is very little specific information as to what happened, what the source of that explosion was, but it’s certainly a reminder that Northern Israel, the upper Galilee and particularly the border with Lebanon remains an area where there is a military operation, with the Israeli military deployed and where thousands of munitions were used over the past 3 years”, Odeh said.
Odeh said the explosion had “mobilised” Israel’s political echelons, with the Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu heading to the area, and the Israeli minister of National Security National Ben Gvir canceling a political engagement that was on his agenda.
Tens of thousands of Israelis living in the country’s north were forced to leave the region after Lebanon’s Hezbollah group started firing rockets following Israel’s genocidal 2023 war in Gaza.
In March, Israeli forces started occupying southern Lebanon following a renewal of hostilities after the US – Israel war on Iran. The military said soldiers and helicopters had been dispatched to the scene in northern Israel, a region from which Israeli forces have been pounding Lebanon, whose Hezbollah militants have fired periodic rockets across the border.
Odeh says most residents have not returned because they “did not have the confidence” that the government will be able to protect them.
“They saw the extensive damage that rockets were exacting on their communities and many them, according reports, have not been encouraged to return because the situation remains volatile”, she said.

articles.title_orig: Are banks, the USPS and stock market open on Columbus Day? Here is what to know.
articles.title_zh: Are banks, the USPS and stock market open on Columbus Day? Here is what to know.
articles.content_orig:
Columbus Day, also known as Indigenous Peoples Day, may be an official federal holiday, but it's not consistently observed across the U.S., according to the Pew Research Center.
Falling on the second Monday in October, the holiday creates a three-day weekend for workers whose employers observe it, including federal employees and some state workers, Pew found.
But a push to shift recognition away from explorer Christopher Columbus and instead honor North America's original inhabitants means the holiday isn't as widely observed as it once was.
Since Oct. 12 is a federal holiday, some services and businesses will be closed. Here's what to know about what is open and closed on Columbus Day/Indigenous Peoples Day.
Yes, Monday, Oct. 12, is a federal holiday, which means that U.S. government offices will be closed and federal workers have the day off.
Yes, the stock market is open on Columbus Day, with neither the New York Stock Exchange nor the Nasdaq market observing it as a holiday.
The stock market will be open during its regular working hours on Monday from 9:30 a.m.-4 p.m. ET.
No, the U.S. Postal Service observes Columbus Day as a holiday, which means there will be no regular residential or business mail delivery. All USPS offices will also be closed.
It's best to check with your bank, as some are open while others observe the holiday.
JPMorgan Chase said that its branches will be open on Oct. 12, but will treat the day as a holiday for online transactions. That means customers can't schedule transactions to occur on Columbus Day, and repeating transactions were processed on the preceding business day.
Many other banks are closed on Columbus Day, including Wells Fargo and Bank of America .
Yes, Costco is open for business today, as Columbus Day isn't among the seven holidays the discount chain observes.
Walmart is also open on Columbus Day, with stores open during regular hours, according to the retailer's website.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
articles.title_zh: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover.
"Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer.
Chipotle's stock was down nearly 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were 1% higher.
The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies.
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.
Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025 , when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.
The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports.
Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

articles.title_orig: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy joins 'America's Newsroom' to express his support for President Donald Trump's energy ceasefire, calling it a 'good first step' toward ending the war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Fox News on Monday that Russia continued attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure despite President Donald Trump's announcement of what he called an immediate energy ceasefire, accusing Vladimir Putin of rejecting Washington's peace efforts and calling for greater pressure on Moscow.
"We are ready today for energy ceasefire, as President Trump said. But I'm not sure that Putin is ready because even after yesterday's messages from the president about energy ceasefire, Putin attacked our gas infrastructure," Zelenskyy told Bill Hemmer in a live interview on " America's Newsroom ."
Asked whether Ukraine would honor the ceasefire, Zelenskyy answered, "Of course," insisting that Kyiv had already refrained from striking Russian energy facilities overnight.
TRUMP ANNOUNCES IMMEDIATE ENERGY CEASEFIRE BETWEEN RUSSIA AND UKRAINE
A family walks past an apartment building that was hit by a Russian drone, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kharkiv, Ukraine, October 12, 2026. (Thomas Peter/Reuters)
"We didn't attack any energy objects on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there will be an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. And we didn't attack, but Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, infrastructure and other things," he said.
The Ukrainian leader described the attacks as Putin's response to Trump's initiative.
"It was his answer to President Trump. He attacked our energy infrastructure," Zelenskyy said. "The communication from Russia was very clear that they don't know anything about energy ceasefire."
Trump announced Sunday on Truth Social that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate halt to attacks on energy facilities. But Moscow has not confirmed accepting such an agreement, and the precise scope of Trump's proposal remains disputed.
According to Axios reporting Sunday , a White House official said the proposal initially focused on halting attacks on oil refineries, with a broader ceasefire covering power plants and electricity grids potentially following. The official acknowledged that Russia had not yet agreed.
UKRAINE STRIKES DEEP INTO RUSSIA’S ARCTIC GAS HEARTLAND AS TRUMP PUSHES PUTIN TOWARD PEACE
Firefighters work at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on October 12, 2026. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)
During the interview, Hemmer pressed Zelenskyy on whether Ukraine would halt attacks on Russia's extensive oil-refining network, which has become a point of contention between Washington and Kyiv amid rising global fuel prices.
Zelenskyy argued that a ceasefire limited to refineries would fail to address Ukraine's greatest vulnerability: its electricity supply.
"When we speak about energy ceasefire, it means only one thing: that they don't attack our energy infrastructure, and we don't respond to their energy infrastructure. This is called energy ceasefire."
Asked again whether Ukrainian forces would refrain from targeting Russian refineries, Zelenskyy gave a conditional commitment. "If Russia will not attack our energy, we will not attack the energy," he said.
Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries , arguing that they contribute to higher fuel prices. On Friday, he announced an agreement with Russia to release diesel supplies to the U.S. and global markets, a decision that drew criticism from lawmakers concerned about providing Moscow with additional revenue.
Zelenskyy challenged Trump's assessment of what is driving diesel prices, pointing instead to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz .
"Everybody understands that the price on diesel doesn't depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia," Zelenskyy told Hemmer. "Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking of Hormuz Strait."
NEW RISK FOR US CONSUMERS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS THREATEN A SECOND MAJOR OIL CHOKEPOINT
A rescuer takes shelter at the entrance of an apartment building amid the threat of another Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on October 12, 2026. (Sofiia Gatilova/Reuters)
The interview also exposed tensions over Trump's calls for Ukraine to hold new presidential elections.
Over the weekend, Trump criticized Zelenskyy and suggested Ukraine needed a new president, arguing that Kyiv had missed opportunities to reach a negotiated settlement with Russia.
"If President Trump wants to change the leader in Ukraine, he has to know that only our people can change," Zelenskyy responded.
The Ukrainian president said he was willing to organize an election but argued that voting remained impossible without a substantial pause in hostilities.
"I'm ready for elections. Really, we need a minimum 60 days for security of infrastructure to prepare for elections," he said.
Zelenskyy described continuing Russian drone and missile attacks as an immediate threat to voters. "We are speaking about thousands of drones, ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, how can people vote?" he asked.
"It's not even about the law. The law is very important. But we speak first of all about security."
He also said he last spoke directly with Trump in New York during the U.N. General Assembly in late September.
ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE
President Donald Trump and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy shake hands as they meet on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City in this handout released September 22, 2026. (Ukrainian Presidential Press Service/Handout via Reuters)
The interview came after another series of Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities and residential areas.
Ukraine's charge d'affaires in Washington, Denys Sienik, said Sunday that Russian forces struck a power plant in Kyiv, disrupting electricity and water supplies, before attacking a thermal power plant in Kharkiv following Trump's announcement.
"In total, over the course of the week, Russia struck electricity generation and transmission facilities more than 200 times," Sienik wrote on X on Oct. 11, 2026.
East2West News agency reported Monday that three civilians — a 16-year-old boy and two women, ages 19 and 51 — were killed in a strike near a grocery store in the Kharkiv region. The agency also reported that five people were wounded in an attack on a residential high-rise.
In Pisochyn, a woman described witnessing the bombardment of a power plant shortly after Trump's announcement, according to East2West. "We believed the statement that they wouldn't strike energy infrastructure," she said. "Just ten minutes after that promise was made, there were already five strikes."
The agency also reported a Ukrainian strike on a Russian military base in occupied Khrustalnyi, in the Luhansk region, where three large fires were reportedly visible. The damage and casualty figures could not be independently confirmed.
Reuters separately reported Monday that Russia continued striking Ukrainian energy targets despite Trump's announcement, while Kyiv maintained that it had refrained from attacking Russian refineries.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, meanwhile, rejected the prospect of a 60-day ceasefire to facilitate Ukrainian elections, arguing that European countries would use the pause to replenish Ukraine's weapons supplies.
"I don't think he deserves a respite," Lavrov said Monday, according to the BBC.
UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS

Privacy Policy | About Our Ads
The International Festivals & Events Association honored Kailua Village during  the 71st Annual IFEA Convention & Expo last week.
The International Festivals & Events Association (IFEA) announced and recognized historic Kailua Village as a 2026 IFEA World Festival & Event City during the 71st Annual IFEA Convention & Expo last week.
The prestigious IFEA World Festival & Event City Award was created to encourage, support, and recognize positive local environments for festivals and events worldwide. Festivals and events generate tremendous cultural, social, and economic value for the communities they serve, but their long-term success depends on strong partnerships and support at every level.
Nestled along the storied Kona Coast of Hawaiʻi Island, historic Kailua Village was once the seat of Hawaiian royalty and home to iconic landmarks such as Huliheʻe Palace and Mokuaikaua Church. It now serves as a dynamic gathering place for residents and visitors alike.
Whether its internationally recognized events such as the Ironman World Championship and Kona Coffee Cultural Festival or beloved community traditions, including Independence Day and Christmas parades, Kailua Village embraces the power of festivals and events to connect people.
Kailua Village demonstrates authentic Hawaiian spirit and commitment to community-driven celebrations, which enrich place and people.
“Through this program, we aim to strengthen the dialogue between events and cities around the globe, at a time when that connection has never been more important,” said IFEA President and CEO Steven Wood Schmader, CFEE, during the award presentations. “The high caliber of this year’s entries highlights the powerful role that festivals and events play in shaping vibrant, sustainable communities. The cities being honored in 2026 are setting strong examples we hope others will follow.”
Entries were reviewed by an international panel of industry experts, making this recognition the only global honor of its kind. Each city’s submission was evaluated on a comprehensive range of criteria, including:
The IFEA World Festival & Event City Award provides an international platform for communities to recognize the success of their ongoing efforts, encourage continued enhancement of festival and event infrastructure, policies, and processes, and showcase their communities as welcoming destinations for festivals and events.
For more information about the 2026 IFEA World Festival & Event City Award recipients, including recipient videos and award presentation photos, visit the IFEA World Festival & Event City Award website.

New Skeleton Horsemen thunder into the Old World
Fresh legions of skeleton soldiers have raised by the will of the Tomb Kings, but they’re not alone. The armies of Khemri boasted squadrons of skilled cavalry, and now their desiccated remains saddle up for another charge across the sands.
This new multipart plastic kit contains 10 cavalry miniatures that can be built as either Skeleton Horsemen or Skeleton Horse Archers, each offering a different tactical option. The Horsemen can be armed with either a cavalry spear or sword to go with their shields, and the kit includes interchangeable heads, making it easy to customise your undead hordes.
You can run these miniatures as a single unit of 10 or two smaller units of five, and each set of five has enough parts to build a full command section including a champion, musician,* and banner bearer – whether Horsemen or Horse Archers.
As the unstoppable Khemrian legions march forwards with ranks of shielded warriors and regiments of archers filling the sky with deadly arrows, the Skeleton Horsemen and Horse Archers fill a vital skirmishing role by using their raw speed to sweep around enemy flanks before hitting them where it hurts the most. They’re especially effective at picking off war engine teams and vulnerable support units, while your heavier units fight over the centre ground.
The new Skeleton Horsemen will be riding into action soon. Grab a copy of Warhammer: The Old World – Ravening Hordes so that you have the rules you need to use the new miniatures in your games.
* And for those asking how can a skeleton blow a trumpet when they don’t have any lungs, the answer is simple – magic.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo to be hospitalized Tuesday for surgery to remove a lung nodule
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo to be hospitalized Tuesday for surgery to remove a lung nodule
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to a hospital Tuesday morning to undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule discovered during recent medical tests, the Vatican said Monday.
The timing of the procedure was confirmed after the 71-year-old American pontiff had a full day of meetings, audiences and appointments.
The Vatican press office also said no particular issue precipitated the tests, denying Italian media reports suggesting an inflammation had prompted the medical check-up.
Leo revealed the discovery during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors’ advice to remove the nodule “in the coming days.” The Vatican predicted a weeklong recovery.
It was business as usual at the Vatican on Monday, with Leo presiding over six private audiences, including with the head of the U.S. military chaplains, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, and one group audience. He also made three appointments, and the Vatican released a letter he had penned to the outgoing dean of the College of Cardinals.
In the afternoon, he was expected to rejoin a weeklong conference he convened on ministering to families.
Leo’s surgery marks the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. It was significant because the pope himself revealed the news, in perhaps the most public way possible: at the end of his Sunday noon blessing, with thousands of people in St. Peter’s Square.
The Vatican has for centuries zealously guarded the pope’s health and has often sent out confusing information, or none at all, about papal illnesses. Pope Francis tried to change that by being upfront about his frailties and musing on his eventual death. But even during his pontificate, information was tightly controlled.
Leo’s decision and reveal suggested an unusual level of transparency by the American pope.
A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. A nodule can be benign or malignant, and oftentimes surgical removal is recommended to ascertain whether it is cancerous since performing a lung biopsy by needle can be difficult.
Oncologists say if the nodule turns out to be cancerous, Leo’s prognosis is “excellent” since it will have been removed at an early stage.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background
articles.title_zh: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background
articles.content_orig:
Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context.
There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns.
Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time.
The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin.
Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting note-takers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day.
Meeting note-taking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself.
The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another.
“The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” the company’s co-founder and CEO, Mo, told TechCrunch.
The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar.
The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information.
Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third-parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech.
Some meeting note-takers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversation and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Voice Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns .
Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem.
“We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said.
Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. The company is hiring for its go-to-market function and AI engineers for working on speech recognition models.

WLOS — The rainfall totals have been reported after the remnants of Isaias swept through western North Carolina from Oct. 10-11, and two areas in western North Carolina reported over 8 inches of rain.
Rainfall totals from Isaias: Parts of western North Carolina get over 8 inches. (WLOS)
Sugar Hill Fire Department in Marion had the highest total since Saturday, reporting 8.32 inches. There were reports of flooding and mudslides over the weekend in McDowell County.
Busick in Yancey County had the second-highest total, with 8.17 inches. Busick was one of the hardest hit areas in WNC by Helene in September 2024. According to data from the National Hurricane Center Tropical Cyclone Report, from Sept. 25-28, Busick recorded 30.78 inches of rain.
MCDOWELL COUNTY FIRE CREW 'RESPONDED LIKE NORMAL' TO 5 LANDSLIDES OVERNIGHT
Crooked Creek in Henderson County was third on News 13's list with 7.88 inches of rain from remnants of Isaias, and Mount Mitchell was next with 7.53 inches. Ridgecrest reported 7.17 inches of rain since Oct. 10, and McDowell Emergency Operations Center reported 6.92 inches.
Lake Lure, another area heavily damaged by Helene, had 6.51 inches of rain, which prompted officials to open the dam’s tainter gates to three feet. This increased the amount of water flowing into the Broad River.
BAT CAVE RESIDENT EXPRESSES CONCERN AS BROAD RIVER LEVELS REMAIN ELEVATED
Hendersonville reported 6.38 inches of rain, and the Asheville Regional Airport reported 4.39 inches.
News 13's weather forecast calls for temperatures to rise back into the low 80s for the rest of the week, with a warm, dry pattern. Rivers and streams are expected to fall back quickly to normal levels and flows.

articles.title_orig: US Homeland Security defends Nidal Hasan livestream execution bid
articles.title_zh: US Homeland Security defends Nidal Hasan livestream execution bid
articles.content_orig:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) chief has defended a plan to livestream the execution of convicted killer Nidal Hasan, rejecting claims that it could fuel radicalisation or make him a martyr.
"I don't see an elevated risk," Markwayne Mullin said on Sunday. "I think people need to understand that if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime."
Hasan, a former US Army Major, is due to be executed by firing squad in December for shooting dead 13 soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Trump administration has said it plans to livestream his death, prompting shock and concern from both Republicans and Democrats.
President Donald Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made.
It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century.
The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week , has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts.
Alaskan Republican Senator, Lisa Murkowski, called the decision "gruesome" and said livestreaming an execution was something she would expect "from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America".
"It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks," she wrote on X , adding that "how we carry out justice matters just as much as the justice itself."
Virginia Democrat Mark Warner said that allowing the public to tune into the execution could heighten the national security risk.
"Beyond the profound moral concerns, a public execution could hand terrorist organizations a propaganda victory, fuel radicalization, and put American service members, diplomats, and citizens overseas at greater risk," he wrote .
But speaking to CBS news programme Face the Nation on Sunday, the DHS secretary rejected these concerns, and insisted the risks had been considered.
"[Hasan] killed 13 individuals on Fort Hood. I have no sympathy for him, and I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies," Mullin told presenter Margaret Brennan.
Nidal Hasan, a former US Army major and psychiatrist from Virginia, admitted to fatally shooting 13 unarmed troops at a crowded medical building at the Fort Hood military base. A further 32 others were injured in the attack.
In court, Hasan apologised for "any mistakes" and said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair.
His execution would be the first by the US military since 1961, and the military's first execution by firing squad since World War Two.

articles.title_orig: Diné paddler honors his roots on the world stage
articles.title_zh: Diné paddler honors his roots on the world stage
articles.content_orig:
From Gallup to Singapore, Adam Becenti has found cultural connection, spiritual strength and community through competitive paddling
From Gallup to Singapore, Adam Becenti has found cultural connection, spiritual strength and community through competitive paddling
Adam Becenti, a Diné paddler from Gallup, is celebrating Indigenous Peoples Day by honoring his roots and showcasing his abilities on the global stage.
Becenti grew up playing sports commonly offered in the New Mexico desert while also participating in Diné ceremonies and learning about his culture from his father.
After moving to Portland, Oregon, in 2013, he joined a Native dragon boat team made up of Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission employees. He began outrigger canoeing in 2017, eventually finding that paddling offered more than exercise and competition.
For Becenti, the sport provides mental, physical, emotional and spiritual benefits while connecting him with Indigenous paddling traditions around the world.
"As a Diné person, we hold water sacred," Becenti said. "Every time I get on the water, I try to make an offering and ultimately connect in those ways."
Paddling has taken Becenti to Japan and New Zealand, where he has learned from other cultures and built relationships with Indigenous communities. He said those experiences showed him that paddling is more than a sport; it is a culture, lifestyle and generational tradition for many Indigenous peoples.
In August, Becenti represented the United States and the Pacific Northwest at the 2026 World Sprints. His team reached the semifinals in its strongest races.
Although the team did not advance as far as it had hoped, Becenti said competing alongside some of the world’s top paddlers and participating in cultural exchanges felt like a victory.
Now living in Seattle, Becenti paddles on Lake Washington and plans to train for distance championships and attempt to qualify for future sprint championships.
His advice to others is to travel, embrace new experiences and build relationships with people from different cultures without forgetting who they are or where they come from.
