articles.title_orig: Real-World Nonhormonal Therapy Effects on VMS Bother, Work, and Mood
articles.title_zh: Real-World Nonhormonal Therapy Effects on VMS Bother, Work, and Mood
articles.content_orig:
Pauline M. Maki, PhD, reviews early OPTION-VMS findings showing improvements in hot flash bother, work productivity, depression, and anxiety with fezolinetant (Veozah).
Pauline M. Maki, PhD, reviews the first data cuts from OPTION-VMS, released at The Menopause Society 2025 meeting. These analyses examined bother from VMS, meaning hot flashes and night sweats, using the MENQOL, a commonly used measure of vasomotor symptom (VMS) bother, along with a widely used measure of workplace productivity. 1
She describes the results as very reassuring because they replicated what was seen in the trials. Where the SKYLIGHT trials showed benefits of fezolinetant (Veozah) on VMS frequency and severity, the original OPTION-VMS data cut showed improvement in women's reported bother from hot flashes. The primary time point was 12 weeks, Maki notes, but improvement was also observed at 4 and 8 weeks, indicating early benefit. In what she calls a critically important outcome, women also reported a substantial boost within 12 weeks in workplace productivity and in activity levels outside of work. This suggests, she explains, that relief from hot flashes and hot flash bother translates to real-world improvement in women's ability to function in daily life.
Maki then turns to new outcome data presented at the Endocrine Society meeting in 2026 on the effects of fezolinetant and other nonhormonal interventions for VMS on depression and anxiety. The study used the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, widely used measures that many providers already have access to in their clinics. Because participants presented to clinics seeking care for VMS, Maki explains, most did not have substantial depression or anxiety at baseline, and levels at the first study visit were minimal. Even with this minimal burden, depression and anxiety improved with fezolinetant after 12 weeks. 2 As a researcher in women's mental health, she finds this especially interesting, and says it suggests secondary benefits for women whose bothersome menopause symptoms are effectively treated.
In the next segment, Maki explains how wrist-worn actigraphy captures sleep problems women underreport and what it shows with fezolinetant vs SSRIs and SNRIs.

Mato is a media platform that uses AI to help companies turn their expertise into professionally produced podcasts and media.
“We’re building the first generation of AI talents that interview real humans, creating authentic content at a scale that was never before possible,” it states.
Mato has been awarded an ElevenLabs grant, received AWS Activate credits and is a member of NVIDIA Inception.
Alexander Benz is co-founder and CEO.
Radio World: What is Mato?
Alexander Benz: Mato is a Los Angeles-based media technology company founded in 2024 by my husband, Edward Benz, and me. The company is privately held, and we recently raised a pre-seed investment from Mucker Capital and joined MuckerLab .
Mato gives companies AI agents that interview real human guests live. The AI host prepares for the subject, conducts an unscripted interview, listens to what the guest actually says, and asks followup questions in real time. The conversation can then move through editing, transcripts, clips, cover art and distribution, with the customer retaining final approval.
RW: Tell us more about it and how it might be used by radio broadcasters or related audio fields.
Benz: The core product is the live AI interviewer.
Most AI audio tools start with text and generate something from it. Mato starts with a person. A real guest joins an interview, speaks naturally, and the AI host conducts the conversation in real time.
A public demonstration of the AI interviewer is available , which includes a Kevin DeMeritt interview, transcript and follow-up timestamps.
For radio, I think the interesting part is what that does to the economics and logistics of producing expert-led audio. A broadcaster can capture interviews, recurring expert segments, branded programming or niche shows without needing a human host and full production team around every recording session.
Since we first spoke, we’ve brought this into traditional radio with Lear Capital. Their Mato-produced show “ Outside the Dollar ” uses AI-hosted interviews with real guests and is now being distributed for radio as well as digital listening.
RW: What prompted the development of a tool that uses an AI host to conduct interviews?
Benz: We were much more interested in whether AI could conduct a good conversation than whether it could generate another piece of content.
There is an enormous amount of useful knowledge sitting inside companies with founders, customers, executives and subject-matter experts. Traditional podcast production makes capturing that knowledge relatively expensive and operationally heavy.
The question became: What happens if the AI does the preparation, interviewing and much of the production work, while the expertise still comes from an actual person?
RW: How do your guardrails assure that the final interview is correct and appropriate?
Benz: We do not claim that an AI interviewer can guarantee that every statement a guest makes is factually correct.
Our approach is to preserve provenance and human editorial control instead.
The recorded human conversation remains the source. Customers can set the subject, questions and editorial boundaries before an interview, and they retain final approval before anything is released. The transcript and recording also make it possible to review the finished material against what the guest actually said.
The AI is responsible for conducting and processing the conversation. It does not become the authority on the subject being discussed.
RW: What is the experience of being interviewed by an AI host like?
Benz: It feels much closer to being interviewed by a person than completing a questionnaire or talking to a traditional chatbot.
The guest joins, the AI host asks a question, and the guest answers naturally. While they are speaking, the agent is listening to the substance of the answer and deciding what makes sense to ask next.
So if someone introduces an unexpected detail, the host can follow that thread rather than simply moving to question number three on a predetermined list.
The guest does not need to write prompts or learn how to use an AI tool. Their job is simply to talk about what they know.
RW: How can an interested reader learn more or hear an example?
Benz: Lear Capital’s “Outside the Dollar” is a useful current example because it shows the model in an actual subject-matter interview rather than a scripted demonstration.
We also have several public interviews and product examples available through Mato, along with a press kit containing screenshots and company information.
RW: What else should we know?
Benz: The distinction that matters most to us is that we are not trying to synthesize the human out of media.
There are already plenty of AI products that can generate an article, a voice or a podcast from a prompt. Mato is built around the opposite premise: The interesting material should still come from a real person.
We want AI to remove much of the coordination and production work required to capture that person’s knowledge, rather than replacing the person whose knowledge made the content worth producing in the first place.
Podcasting is our first use case, but we see the broader product as a conversation layer for capturing human knowledge.

articles.title_orig: WATCH: Pope Leo XIV Marks 100 Years of World Mission Sunday
articles.title_zh: WATCH: Pope Leo XIV Marks 100 Years of World Mission Sunday
articles.content_orig:
In a new video for the centennial, Pope Leo reflects on his personal connection to World Mission Sunday, from his childhood in the United States to his years of missionary service in Peru.
Ahead of the 100th World Mission Sunday on the weekend of October 17-18, Pope Leo XIV released a personal video message reflecting on the extraordinary day.
100 years ago, when World Mission Sunday began, there were about 9.6 million Catholics living in 296 mission jurisdictions. Today, that number has grown to more than 346 million Catholics living in 1,131 mission territories.
These individuals are served through more than 41,000 parishes, 124,309 Catholic schools and 26, 318 social institutions.
When he was a child, Pope Leo XIV celebrated World Mission Sunday in the United States. Later, when he was a priest and bishop in Peru, he was the recipient of the generous prayers and support of Catholics around the world.
Now, as pope, he celebrates the centennial of the mission-supporting international collection and expresses gratitude for the Church's loving support of our brothers and sisters worldwide.
To support World Mission Sunday, Catholics across Northern Colorado may donate to their parish with "World Mission Sunday" in the memo line of their donation. For more information, visit the Pontifical Mission Societies' website here .

articles.title_orig: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
articles.title_zh: The man hiking the world in search of rare cheeses
articles.content_orig:
Trevor Warmedahl has spent years documenting rare and traditional cheesemaking methods, and believes that "cheese is an edible manifestation of a place".
Trevor Warmedahl was working as a commercial cheesemaker in Seattle when he realised he was using milk that came from animals he never saw. So, he quit his job and set off on what has become a global odyssey to discover places that still make cheese the old-fashioned way.
In 2019 he arrived in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, and lived alone in a yurt with a dog as his companion. He soon discovered that dairy was sacred there: the women flicked milk into the air before cheesemaking, a gesture of respect called a milk libation . He visited homes where whey bubbled over central hearths and fresh, unripened byaslag cheese covered tables. After hiking to shrines, he noticed people offered dairy products as a symbol of purity.
As summer unfolded and city-dwellers migrated to the Mongolian steppe to farm, Warmedahl itched to join. He jumped on a Soviet-era coal-powered sleeper train for a rickety overnight ride across the Gobi Desert. On the journey back to Ulaanbaatar, he met a local who invited him to stay with her herder family on the Zavkhan grassland.
Warmedahl spent that summer waking before dawn to milk yaks, chasing livestock up the valley on horses, listening to shepherds' folk songs at sunset and cooking milk into dehydrated, sweet-and-sour curds called aaruul . The experience inspired him to seek out other places preserving rare cheesemaking traditions before they disappeared.
During the past six years, Warmedahl has hitched, hiked and driven through more than 20 countries, documenting traditional cheesemaking and pastoral lifestyles, and offering workshops on natural dairy processing . After recently completing a 193km (120-mile) cheese trek across the Peaks of the Balkans Trail , he shared with the BBC what cheesemaking reveals about a place.
You've been to so many places – Bulgaria, Pakistan, Italy, Austria, Cambodia. Share a standout adventure.
Ancestral cheeses in Georgia have no analogues – I call them "fossil cheeses" because they were almost lost but are making a comeback as part of a broader post-Soviet cultural revival. My pinnacle moment happened in Tusheti, a mountain region bordering Russia near the tourist village of Omalo.
I showed up with vague directions to the shepherds' summer camp, which was deep in the valley. That's a theme: the cheeses I find are always far out, made by hermit types sticking to the old ways out of sheer stubbornness. It was drop-dead gorgeous, just me and my backpack. The valley ends on an abrupt cliff, with deteriorating medieval stone towers. Shepherds build their camps from the decay. I saw how these guys milked sheep by hand with wooden pails, rustic-style. It's a feta-like cheese called Tushuri guda , aged in inside-out sheepskins. At the end of the season, I walked about 130km (81 miles) back down the valley with them and 300 sheep. The herd has done this for generations – they know where to go. The shepherds just coordinated, and it created this crazy lawless feeling with dogs barking and me, chasing stray sheep down ravines.
At night we'd build a campfire and drink, and even with the language barrier, we'd relate through food. Sometimes language isn't needed. In cheesemaking, if two hearts want to connect, they'll find a way.
How is cheese and cheesemaking a reflection of a community's history and culture?
Cheese is a sensory experience and embodies larger ideas about how we live. It represents how meaningful human cultures can be. At its best, cheese reflects this complex relationship between humans, landscapes, microbial life and livestock at a time [when] we've become so separate from how food is made. And the cultural element holds the constellation together.
The cheeses I highlight represent an older mentality, with a sense of stewardship over the places we live and farm. So, a little bit more of the wildness of nature slips into the product. [Cheese is] an edible manifestation of place, of cultural history transformed into delicious food.
Why is cheesemaking especially important today?
The diversity and range of cheese is infinite. When animals eat, they transform grass and entire landscapes into milk that becomes cheese, and animals can graze [almost] anywhere. So, it's a lifestyle that can move in response to climate uncertainty and desertification – real challenges today.
The cheeses I focus on – natural farmstead cheeses [made exclusively with milk from a farmer's own animals] – reflect deep, ethical relationships between people and livestock and highlight the incredible diversity of heritage livestock. With industrialisation, that diversity is vanishing at an alarming rate. So pastoral cheesemaking strikes me as profoundly sustainable.
What can so-called "exotic cheeses" that challenge us reveal about a place?
There's this greyish-brown cheese from Norway, gammelost , [covered in] moulds like fruit rot. It tastes like a musty cellar with bold, mouth-numbing spiciness. It wasn't for me. But deliciousness is cultural. It's taught. So, I always say: don't try something once, try it 10 times. Uncomfortable foods open doors. But be sure to eat them because you're interested in the culture, not because they're freaky to you.
One of the easiest ways to express interest in a culture is to say: feed me what you eat. When people realise you're genuine, the relationship deepens and you begin to understand their history through food. Funky cheeses become cultural emblems because of how obscure and special they are.
You set out on your global cheese journey without a real plan. What did this approach add to your experience?
Back then [in 2019], I was hopping on a whim from one volunteer gig to the next, drawn to remote places where people worked to protect and revitalise traditional cheeses. Workaway on farms, or staying for a while at guesthouses where cheese is made, are still amazing ways to go beyond tourism to see how people really live.
Cheese gives you access to a global community, like at [the Slow Food Cheese Festival in] Bra, Italy. But anything you can do to find that deeper experience – food, handicrafts – is worth it, even if you can't always plan in advance. If your heart is in the right place and you jump fully into adventure when it calls, the details will almost always work themselves out.
What advice would you give fellow travellers about how to best experience unique cheeses abroad?
Find the cheese shop or cheesemonger that has the most local tilt and ask them which cheesemakers you can and should visit. Organising it yourself is cheaper. But there are also paid tours where you can experience a range of cheeses in a short period and really get to know a place. Just make sure that the cost actually supports local producers – that's what I call responsible "lacto-culinary" tourism.
How can other travellers seek out responsible agrotourism experiences?
Look for local cheesemakers and guides. It's also important to not expect farmers to sanitise things. It's normal to go to a farm and see broken-down equipment and mud. When we romanticise tradition, it encourages locals to put themselves in a museum. But tools [and] tradition have always evolved.

We need to be open to the fact that it's not all grandmas spinning wool on wheels outside stone cottages. Then it becomes kind of a show, and we're pushing farmers to become something they're not for tourists.
What places have exciting, overlooked, or under-the-radar cheeses? Where are you keen to travel next?
Hands down, Turkey . It's a universe of cheese that doesn't get enough attention. Tulum peyniri is emblematic of pastoral lifestyles and the extreme sacrifice at the root of dairying and – I'd argue – life. That's because it's aged mainly in furry goatskins, so it looks insane bec

articles.title_orig: A Mysterious Signal Reached Us From When The Universe Was Just 3 Billion Years Old. Its Home Galaxy Surprised Astronomers.
articles.title_zh: A Mysterious Signal Reached Us From When The Universe Was Just 3 Billion Years Old. Its Home Galaxy Surprised Astronomers.
articles.content_orig:
Sometimes we receive strange, ghostly radio signals from outer space, which astronomers have yet to conclusively explain.
Partially because they disappear almost as soon as they arrive.
The ephemera known as fast radio bursts (FRBs) are among the Universe's most mysterious occurrences, even more eerie than the supposed little green aliens with a penchant for physical probes.
If they were related, that would neatly solve two major mysteries.
But FRBs are bursts of radio waves from the distant cosmos, generally lasting for tiny fractions of a second (i.e., fast).
Their transience, and the fact that they randomly appear across the sky, have made it difficult to pin down their origins for nearly two decades since their discovery in 2007.
But we just got a huge clue: Astronomers have reported the most distant FRB yet, designated FRB 20240304B, a burst of ancient energy that was emitted in one-thousandth of a second and has traveled through 80 percent of the Universe's history to meet us.
"What makes fast radio bursts interesting is that we don't know what generates them," explains lead author Manisha Caleb, a radio astronomer and astrophysicist at the University of Sydney.
"We have theories for what objects produce them, but we don't have conclusive proof."
So, who's the cosmic culprit in this specific case? Possibly a magnetar: a type of neutron star on steroids that packs the most powerful magnetic fields in the Universe and squeezes the mass of a whole Sun into a magnetic marble the size of San Francisco Bay .
Yet here's another conundrum: despite their incomprehensibly intense origins, and their ability to release 500 million Suns' worth of energy in thousandths of a second , they may be light(er)weights compared to other stellar outbursts, which has led to a sampler platter of possibilities and added to the difficulty of their conclusive identification:
"We observationalists can only kill models, never prove them. So, when you have 100 to kill, it takes a fair bit of time."  – astronomer and astrophysicist J. Xavier Prochaska
"Fundamentally, it is because the energies involved are modest. They are extreme for radio wave emission, but nothing like the energy in a supernova or gamma-ray burst," J. Xavier Prochaska, an astronomer and astrophysicist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, told ScienceAlert.
"As such, theorists have devised nearly 100 models to generate them.
"We observationalists can only kill models, never prove them. So, when you have 100 to kill, it takes a fair bit of time."
In the study, published in the journal Science , a massive, international collaboration of astronomers used multiple observatories to explore this mysterious FRB emanating from 'cosmic noon,' an era only 3 billion years after the Big Bang when Universal star formation was at its peak.
The astronomers identified the FRB in March 2024 using MeerKAT , a 64-antenna radio telescope in South Africa's Meerkat National Park.
They then pointed two ultra-sensitive ground telescopes at the corresponding patch of sky to see its host galaxy and discovered… darkness.
They looked as deep as they could "but there was simply nothing to see," Prochaska says .
So they called in the heavy orbital artillery (just a metaphor, for now), the JWST and its exceptional infrared sensitivity.
And if the researchers suspected a monster, they found a mouse:
"We thought it would be a big, nicely formed galaxy with lots of stars, and instead it was a little dwarf galaxy, although it was actively forming stars," says Caleb.
Altogether, this dwarf galaxy is 1,000 times less massive than expected .
It's also exceedingly young, with 90 percent of its stellar mass having formed in the past 30 million years.
This helped the astronomers favor a magnetar as the potential source of the historic FRB.
Another prominent FRB scenario involves the collision of two neutron stars, a cataclysmic crash that yields a black hole or an extra-heavy neutron star , plus a bunch of literal gold .
Yet neutron stars dance around each other for billions of years before colliding, like a still-shy couple on a second date, so it wouldn't make sense in a young galaxy.
Magnetars, however, can form and release their magnetic energy in just millions of years. Especially in a metal-poor galaxy like this that breeds massive stars.
Also, like good guests, FRBs come bearing gifts of the astrophysical kind.
Even though light travels at the speed of itself , the ultimate breakneck physical limit, it only does so in a vacuum.
And as this FRB passed through the cold, ionized (electrically charged) gas that permeates the cosmos, its lower-frequency waves were slowed more than its higher ones, so they arrived later.
Turbulent gas, most likely in its home galaxy, also scattered the signal, smearing it out over several milliseconds
FRBs thus act as an astronomical flashlight , and this particular one has had its signal warped by two cosmic-scale structures as it traversed most of the Universe to meet us.
In doing so, it helped illuminate an unknown galaxy group along the way, located about 3.5 billion light-years away, while also bearing the ionic imprint of the Virgo Cluster, the nearest such structure to Earth, only around 54 million light-years distant.
Finally, since we only know of about 100 FRBs whose host galaxies have been confirmed, the researchers note , and most are billions of light-years more local, this wasn't just the cherry atop the celestial sundae, but a whole other sundae on top of the sundae.
"Because we have scant understanding of what generates FRBs, we could only hope that they might exist at such early times," Prochaska told ScienceAlert.
"Now, we have proven it and this will drive new, dedicated studies to find others – and search even greater distances!"
The research has been published in Science .
This article was fact-checked by Rebecca Dyer and edited by Rebecca Dyer . While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know .

articles.title_orig: Mamdani Rolls Out Police Reforms Related to Use of Force
articles.title_zh: Mamdani Rolls Out Police Reforms Related to Use of Force
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK CITY (WABC) -- Mayor Zohran Mamdani has directed the NYPD to conduct its first comprehensive review of use-of-force policies and practices in a decade and announced a series of reforms aimed at strengthening accountability for officers accused of serious misconduct.
The review, which will take place over the coming months, comes as the administration faces mounting pressure from some supporters to follow through on campaign promises related to policing, including calls to dismantle the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. The mayor also said he has no plans to remove Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch.
According to the mayor's office, the review will include a community engagement process and examine how the department's use-of-force policies are applied and whether changes are needed. The administration said it is the first such review in 10 years.
The announcement was tied in part to the retirement of an officer who was facing disciplinary charges in the death of 19-year-old Win Rozario, who was shot and killed by NYPD officers during a mental health crisis in March 2024. The officer retired before an internal disciplinary trial could take place.
"When the government uses force against a New Yorker, the standard for accountability must be at its highest. Every New Yorker deserves to know that force will be used lawfully, carefully and only when necessary," Mamdani said in a statement.
In addition to the use-of-force review, the administration announced several changes designed to increase oversight and transparency. The city will increase funding for the Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD by $2.6 million, a move the administration said will restore staffing to a historic peak and expand the office's ability to investigate policies and practices related to police misconduct.
The NYPD has also implemented a new notification system intended to help complete disciplinary proceedings before an officer retires. The department will formalize its practice of notifying the state when officers retire while facing disciplinary charges, a step aimed at preventing those officers from joining another law enforcement agency elsewhere in New York.
Other reforms include maintaining compliance with state reporting requirements for police-involved deaths and formalizing how information is shared with the public and families following critical incidents. The NYPD will also release Force Investigation Division final reports to families or their representatives upon request.
The mayor's office said the reforms are intended to ensure serious allegations are investigated, disciplinary cases are resolved, and the public has a clearer understanding of how the city responds when police use of force results in death or serious injury.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
articles.content_orig:
Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences
Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?
Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air and Bahrain Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saaturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.
The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.
The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.
The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising that the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”
He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers. They cannot diversify geography […] when energy infrastructure in this region is targeted, the consequences reach economies everywhere.”
An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences. Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home. The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.
Interceptor missiles are needed to protect government buildings, oil facilities and infrastructure hubs across a wide geographic area. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi airports across the country.
Houthi attacks since last month have targeted fuel tanks at Riyadh airport and its affiliated warehouses, destroying a parked Airbus A320 passenger plane and damaging at least five other aircraft.
The crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, has not been seen in public since Tuesday last week, reflecting the pressure he is under to find a way out from a war that has intermittently dogged his leadership since 2014. Saudi Arabia badly needs stability to continue the slow diversification of its economy from oil dependence, but has not found a way to restore it in Yemen .
Inside Yemen, fighting continued in and around Taiz, the third city, and the most populous governorate, with Saudi planes mounting eight separate strikes on any assembly of Houthi forces. As many as 60 fighters died on Sunday from both sides.
The governor of Taiz, Nabil Shamsan, on Sunday issued an urgent call to lift the Houthi siege and warned a shortage of medicines meant the city would soon run out of emergency surgical and intensive care services.
Overall the Houthis claimed the Saudis had mounted 124 raids on Sunday. The Saudis are seeking to locate Abdul-Malik al-Houthi, the reclusive leader of the Houthis, with rumours of his assassination repeatedly circulating, but Saudi Arabia does not seem to have contemporary intelligence on his precise whereabouts either in the capital Sana’a or in its stronghold of Saada.
On the diplomatic front, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, spoke to the Saudi foreign minister, Faisal bin Farhan, on Sunday to see if there was a way in which Iran could act as a mediator between the Saudis and the Houthis, a group that Iran has trained and armed. Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau claimed Saudi Arabia accepted the mediation offered by Iran and proposed first a one-month truce, and then a two week truce, but the Houthis had rejected both offers.
He said “the battle this time is not like its predecessors; the arena is no longer the same arena, and the cards have changed. Therefore, a comprehensive settlement must be put in place between Riyadh and Sana’a, the Houthi capital because every day that passes in this battle will expand its scope and deepen its losses, and the settlement that is possible today may become difficult or impossible tomorrow”.
A meeting of the UN security council in New York on Tuesday is expected to debate a resolution calling the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation.
The exiled leader of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), Aidarous al-Zubaidi, called for southern forces to fight on all fronts, and not just to defend the borders of the former South Yemen, in a move that is likely to be welcomed by Saudi Arabia as it supports the week-old call by the UN-recognised government to drive the Houthis out of the whole of Yemen, rather than just from the southern governorates.
The STC has a vision of an independent South Yemen that would recreate the separate state that existed between 1967 and 1990. The reunification of Yemen at the end of the cold war proved fragile and many southerners nurse longstanding grievances about the distribution of resources in the unified state.
The STC’s authority has been challenged by Abd al-Rahman al-Mahrami, the Salafist leader who commands the powerful Southern Giants Brigades.
Despite Araghchi’s efforts to reach out to the Saudis, Mohsen Rezaei, the more hardline secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, claimed Iran was hitting five or six small vessels in the strait of Hormuz every night, explaining the vessels were being used by the Emirati military to move oil through the strait to larger tankers, thus breaching the blockade that Iran is seeking to maintain to push up oil prices and weaken Donald Trump .
Esmail Baghaei, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, said Trump’s treatment of Volodymyr Zelenskyy, including his call for the Ukrainian president to stand aside showed the risks in dealing with Trump. He said: “Being an enemy of America can be dangerous, but being a friend of America is deadly. You can see for yourself what America’s friendship and enmity with its allies is like.”

articles.title_orig: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
articles.title_zh: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
articles.content_orig:
English English (pdf) Swedish Swedish (pdf)
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel 2026 to
Robert E. Hall Stanford University, CA, USA.
Michael Woodford Columbia University, New York, USA.
“for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”
This year’s laureates in the economic sciences, Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, have developed new macroeconomic models that have significantly improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy. On the basis of these models, well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures can reduce the economy’s peaks and troughs.
The economy is characterised by alternating downturns and upturns. Ever since the economist John Maynard Keynes launched his theories almost a century ago, stabilisation policy has been important for tackling these fluctuations. During recessions, the economy is boosted by reducing interest rates and increasing the budget deficit, while the opposite should be done to slow a booming economy.
However, during the oil crises of the 1970s, it seemed that the Keynesian models that govern when and how measures should be implemented no longer worked. They did not reduce unemployment, but led to uncontrolled inflation instead. The West experienced a decade of low growth, high unemployment and high inflation. Many people believed that stabilisation policy had done more harm than good and that it should be retired.
Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are awarded this year’s prize in economic sciences for demonstrating how economic models could be reconstructed to revitalise stabilisation policy. Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation. This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.
A central component in these models is that households and businesses are forward looking when making decisions about savings or product prices. When governments and central banks communicate their plans for economic policy, they can influence this view of the future and move the economy in the right direction. Since the new models’ introduction, they have been extremely helpful in dealing with the economic downturns that have affected us.
“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world. With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume,” says John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences.

articles.title_orig: World Thrombosis Day: Why conversations about patient risk matter
articles.title_zh: World Thrombosis Day: Why conversations about patient risk matter
articles.content_orig:
In a hospital ward, the greatest risks to a patient's recovery are rarely static warning signs; they are shifting variables that often develop unseen. Although some factors are visible at admission, others emerge only as a patient’s condition changes. That is why continuous monitoring throughout the patient journey is important. World Thrombosis Day (October 13) brings this to the forefront. Each year, this global campaign draws attention to the hidden dangers of venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE).
VTE remains a persistent global challenge. A review published in Research and Practice in Thrombosis and Haemostasis describes VTE as a leading cause of preventable illness and death associated with hospitalization. The review also estimates that as many as 60% of VTE cases occur during a hospital stay or within 90 days after discharge.
VTE prevention is an important area of focus, but identifying who may be at risk is not always straightforward. Factors such as a history of VTE, active cancer or limited mobility may be evident at admission, while others can emerge following surgery, prolonged immobility, infection or changes in a patient’s overall condition.
When VTE occurs, the effects can be significant. According to the American Heart Association , VTE can contribute to longer hospital stays and is a leading cause of preventable death among hospitalized patients. Extended stays may also reduce the availability of beds and resources for other patients.
This is why preventive care matters. Rather than being a one-time consideration, it involves looking ahead and regularly assessing and monitoring VTE risk as a patient moves through the care journey. This approach can help clinical teams ask relevant questions at different points in patient care and support informed clinical decision-making.
Throughout October, Cardinal Health is inviting healthcare professionals across more than 30 markets worldwide to explore realistic patient scenarios from different specialties and care settings. The scenarios are not intended to offer a single solution. Instead, they are designed to encourage discussion about how VTE risk is identified and monitored. They show how risk factors can vary from one patient to another and how important it is to look beyond what is immediately visible.
World Thrombosis Day is an opportunity to raise awareness and keep these conversations going throughout the month and beyond. By sharing our educational resources and patient scenarios, we hope to provide healthcare professionals with practical content that supports informed conversations and decision-making. Our goal is to stand alongside healthcare teams year-round, providing the insights they need to champion patient care, promote efficient care delivery and make effective use of hospital resources.
You can learn more about our World Thrombosis Day educational resources and patient scenarios here .

articles.title_orig: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
articles.title_zh: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
articles.content_orig:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified after organizers concluded that his use of generative AI broke the rules.
Ning Xu was named the winner of the annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition in September, but his video received a number of critical comments from experts who questioned its use of AI.
Nikon launched an investigation, and announced its conclusion in a statement Friday.
“After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI,” the statement reads, adding that the competition rankings have been adjusted.
“This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” it said.
Nikon also said it would revisit its rules and evaluation procedures for the annual competition in future.
The new winner is a video showing a tiny roundworm and a single-celled Dileptus, a kind of single-celled microorganism, by Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat.
Xu’s video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder.
When Nikon posted the video on LinkedIn, it attracted criticism from scientists such as Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, who said there were “many serious problems with this video.”
Winner of Nikon microscopy photo contest faces criticism over AI usage
Phelps said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added.
In response, in a series of comments on LinkedIn, Xu acknowledged that he had used AI.
“AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion,” he wrote.
“It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added.
CNN has reached out to Xu, who now works at the National University of Singapore as a research fellow, for further comment.

articles.title_orig: Sea World starts building marine wildlife hospital on Gold Coast
articles.title_zh: Sea World starts building marine wildlife hospital on Gold Coast
articles.content_orig:
New facility will care for sick and injured marine wildlife
Construction is underway on a new world-class marine wildlife hospital at Sea World in Australia
Construction is underway on a new world-class marine wildlife hospital at Sea World on Australia's Gold Coast.
The new Sea World Foundation Wildlife Hospital is expected to open next year and will serve as the Southern Hemisphere's first facility of its kind.
It will provide specialist care for sick and injured marine wildlife , including dolphins, whales, dugongs, rays, turtles, seabirds and sharks.
Purpose-built for rapid rescue and rehabilitation, the new facility will feature specialist equipment to treat larger marine mammals.
Queensland’s environment minister Andrew Powell said: “Shovels are in the ground at Sea World, with work underway on a world-class marine wildlife hospital that will give more sick and injured wildlife the specialist care they need."
As well as caring for marine wildlife, the hospital will give Sea World visitors the opportunity to see marine conservation and rehabilitation for themselves.
"This is a win for wildlife and a win for Queensland, supporting wildlife rehabilitation while creating new education opportunities and showcasing our conservation efforts to millions of visitors each year," Powell added.
Sea World is owned by Australia-based theme park operator Village Roadshow Group.
The new Sea World Foundation Wildlife Hospital is expected to open next year on the Gold Coast Sea World Foundation
Village Roadshow Group 's CEO Clark Kirby said: "For more than 30 years, Sea World has been at the forefront of marine rescue and rehabilitation efforts around Australia, and this project will allow our team to have an even greater impact on Australian marine life.
“The state-of-the-art facility will allow our specialised veterinary and marine animal experts to help more animals and educate the millions of guests who visit Sea World on conservation efforts to minimise impacts on the environment."
He added: “We have already rescued hundreds of marine animals this year, ranging from whales, dolphins, dugongs, turtles, seabirds and sea snakes, and with marine wildlife being under more threat than before, this new facility will greatly expand our capabilities.”

articles.title_orig: Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
articles.title_zh: Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
articles.content_orig:
Love blooms on a hostile colony world in As You Wake, Break the Shell
Sci-fi author Becky Chambers on designing believable ecosystems, balancing scientific accuracy with emotional impact and emphasizing empathy over spectacle
By Sam Macdonald edited by Sarah Lewin Frasier
One of science fiction’s oldest themes is its insistence that the future isn’t inevitable. Few contemporary authors embody that idea more than Becky Chambers , whose stories imagine alternative futures—not through grand revolutions or galaxy-spanning battles but through ordinary people trying to care for one another.
As a defining voice of the “hopepunk” genre, Chambers has built a reputation for science fiction that prizes empathy as much as imagination. Her latest novel, As You Wake, Break the Shell , brings us to the hostile, unpredictable world of Fortune, where acid rain falls and billowing volcanoes shroud the horizon. The story follows a reclusive botanist and a spacefaring pilot across alternating timelines as they search for connection and purpose, attempting to navigate a life where Fortune has never favored the bold.
We caught up with Chambers to discuss a toxic planet’s world-building, scientific accuracy in storytelling and the motivational merits of unrelenting spite.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
[ An edited transcript of the interview follows .]
This story spends a lot of time on a colony planet with a poisonous atmosphere. What does designing an ecosystem teach you about designing a civilization?
Everything. It’s really important for me to start with what the environmental conditions are because that’s going to affect everything from what we’re eating, what we’re building houses out of, what kind of clothes we have—and all of those things, in turn, affect culture. There is so much about our values, our personalities, that are actually molded by the physical environments we exist in, both natural and constructed.
Starting from [the questions] “what do we have” and “what do we not have” is really important for me. Suppose someone’s eating a sandwich. What’s in the sandwich? It’s a throwaway line that seems like it doesn’t matter, but it’s actually really important to say whether or not there’s lettuce in this sandwich, because that does communicate a lot of information about how this world works.
For this book, I had a really big table of crops [to reference], what are we growing, how are we growing it, what’s available and what’s not?
Those are details I spend a lot of time sussing out before I really get into the thick of drafting the story.
What specific ideas inspired the scientific foundation for this story?
Botany is the big one. I have always had an appreciation for plants but not any actual sort of technical knowledge about what it is that I’m looking at. So I did a lot of research for this book into how plants work, and specifically into seeds, which is a topic I have become fascinated by the more I learn about it. Seeds are a big part of this book, as are plants and the way they communicate with each other.
How does scientific accuracy influence your storytelling? Do you often find yourself molding the plot to fit the science, or vice versa?
I look at science as partially a foundation but more of a tool that I use to color the world that I’m in. I want it to feel tangible and possible, but I’m very willing to take some liberties here and there for the sake of getting the feeling across.
I tend to think of what I’m doing as more like impressionism than photorealism. If you think of something like Monet’s Water Lilies, for example, it doesn’t look like a real pond, right? But it feels like a real pond. And I often use a similar approach with my work. I am not necessarily painting you a picture of the cosmos as it actually exists, but what I’m trying to communicate is the sense of wonder and awe that I feel when I’m experiencing those things in the real world. So it’s a matter of getting the emotional quality of discovery across, and sometimes that does mean taking shortcuts.
With As You Wake Break the Shell , I kept it within the realm of “with sufficient technology, this could be possible.” Is it probable? Probably not. There are a lot of things that I gloss over because they’re not things that everyday people outside of science would know about or understand. We know [in the reality of the story] that there are giant space-dwelling creatures out there. We don’t need to know how it is that they evolved or what kind of world it is that they came from. Those are questions that interest me as a person who is into real science, but they don’t serve the story.
This book has a knack for taking the unknown and making it feel familiar while making the familiar feel unknown, simply by showing it from a new perspective—for instance, that of an enormous, cargo-toting space behemoth. How do you get into the headspace of examining humanity from the outside?
It’s a highly technical process that involves me sitting in my armchair and just staring at the ceiling and thinking about what it would be like to have a body other than mine, and just sort of deconstructing everything that makes me down to the raw components and trying to figure out what it is that’s necessary and what’s not.
I take a lot of inspiration from the natural world. I have a really keen interest in invertebrate life and in deep-sea life, and I have a real interest in animal intelligence that exists in nonmammalian creatures.
What would it mean to communicate through color? What would it mean to communicate through pheromones? What does the world feel like if you don’t have a sense of sight like we do? I just love taking any one of those traits and then expanding it to make something that we would recognize as a person, regardless of whether they physically look like us or not. How does that make you think about yourself? How does that make you think about existence?
As You Wake, Break the Shell is a love story as much as a space story. What did pairing those genres let you explore that you couldn’t do with either one on their own?
It allowed me the freedom to not segment any of the things I was thinking of into separate boxes. This was a really personal book for me in that I’m writing about everything I care about in this one. I’m writing about the natural world, I’m writing about society, and I am also writing about love, romantic love, and these are all things that are extremely important to me in my everyday life.
We have a bazillion stories about “and then they lived happily ever after,” but I actually want to see what that looks like because it’s never that simple.I feel that the most interesting parts of a relationship are what happens “after,” and so that was what drove a large part of my decision to have [the book] be a split timeline, where it’s very clear from the jump that they’re going to be together a long time and we’re going to see all these different stages in what makes them them, because I do think that that’s an area that is underexplored.
You’ve said before that you write the stories that you need to hear. What did you need to hear from this book?
I wanted to see a relationship that matched my own. Queer representation in media is better than ever in a lot of ways, and yet it’s still very rare to see anybody over their 20s.
By the time we started getting more stories about coming of age or people falling in love when they’re young, I was already too old for those stories. I was feeling a real frustration in not finding love stories that spoke to me where I am now in my life. It was one of those things of, “I guess I’ll just have to write it myself.”

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | Quantum-Computing Company IonQ to Buy Cybersecurity Firm for Up to $1.3 Billion
articles.content_orig:
College Park, Md. - Oct. 12, 2026 - IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, today announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Elisity, Inc., a Zero Trust security company, in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion. The acquisition brings together IonQ's post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities with Elisity's enterprise Zero Trust technology platform. On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.
Elisity builds on IonQ’s expanding quantum security offerings with a high-growth enterprise security business, cutting-edge Zero Trust technology platform, and team of industry leaders led by cybersecurity expert CEO James Winebrenner. Elisity has a strong track record of doubling its revenue and its customer base year-over-year with zero churn among deployed customers. With more than 100 global customer deployments and deep CISO and security community relationships, Elisity will provide IonQ with expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation opportunity with double-digit CAGR to IonQ.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ, we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era. As I said first, Q-Day is coming much faster than predicted. IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity. Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.
“Our customers need to prioritize post-quantum cryptography initiatives while securing existing assets to keep essential operations running,” said James Winebrenner, CEO of Elisity. “With IonQ, we will be optimally positioned to partner with them to modernize their crypto-agility programs, accelerate post-quantum cryptography capabilities while advancing their holistic Zero Trust posture and deploy hybrid-cybersecurity solutions today that are prepared for the quantum future.”
Elisity’s Commercial Advantage
Enterprises face two overlapping priorities: containing attacks that operate at machine speed and preparing to protect sensitive information against future quantum threats. The urgency of this transition is underscored by recent White House executive orders advancing quantum innovation and accelerating the federal government's migration to PQC. These directives reinforce the importance of securing critical systems and preparing government networks for quantum-era threats while supporting long-term modernization.
Today, Elisity IdentityGraph combines native asset identity and partner-enriched context, and risk information to inform least-privilege access policy for users, devices, workloads and AI agents. Teams can simulate policies before limiting each identity to the communications it needs, helping reduce attack surface and contain an attack’s spread. By bringing together Elisity's Zero Trust framework with IonQ's PQC and QKD capabilities, the companies will combine cryptographic protection for sensitive information and communications with identity-based controls that limit unauthorized access and the spread of threats across enterprise networks. The shared roadmap with IonQ will extend IdentityGraph with cryptographic inventory and risk information. This integrated approach will help customers address quantum-related security risks through a multiyear transition while strengthening defenses against current cyberattacks, including threats involving AI agents.
Following closing, Elisity will continue serving its customers under its current leadership, including current CEO James Winebrenner. Together, the companies will continue their track record of innovation, customer success and strong partner relationships, backed by IonQ’s demonstrated approach of investing in the critical technologies it acquires.
IonQ’s Multiproduct Revenue Growth Opportunity
IonQ brings an established track record in growing its quantum security and quantum-secure communications offering. The company has deployed some of the largest quantum-safe national communications networks in the world, including in Switzerland, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and serves global customers with quantum-safe defense in depth spanning quantum-safe posture management, quantum key distribution, and post quantum cryptography.
Customers are increasingly adopting multiple IonQ products and services, driving growth in multiproduct revenue and providing evidence of demand for integrated solutions; in the second quarter of 2026, IonQ delivered 40% year-over-year growth in multiproduct revenue..
IonQ and Elisity expect opportunities to cross-sell complementary security solutions, expand relationships with enterprise and government customers, and develop integrated offerings.
Under the terms of the agreement, IonQ will acquire Elisity in an all-stock transaction valued at up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in earnout opportunity subject to performance of the Elisity business. The number of IonQ shares to be issued in the transaction will be calculated at closing based on the volume weighted average price of IonQ common stock for the 20 trading days prior to, but not including, the third business day before the closing date, but that price will not be greater than $49.61 or less than $33.07 per share.
The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of required regulatory approval.
Elisity helps enterprises advance Zero Trust security for users, devices, workloads, AI agents and other non-human identities. Elisity IdentityGraph correlates identity, asset and risk information from native and partner sources to inform access decisions. Elisity’s software policy layer uses the network to enforce access rules independently of the underlying network technology. Teams can simulate policies and limit each identity to the communications it needs, extending the value of existing network and security investments. Founded in 2019, Elisity has a global employee footprint and a growing number of customers in the Fortune 500. Learn more at elisity.com .
IonQ, Inc . [NYSE: IONQ] is the world’s leading quantum platform and foundry - delivering integrated quantum solutions across computing, networking, sensing, and security. IonQ’s newest generation of quantum computers, the Superion, is the latest in a line of cutting-edge systems. Earlier systems have helped customers and partners including Amazon Web Services, AstraZeneca, and NVIDIA achieve a 20x performance increase over previous quantum solutions and accelerate innovation in drug discovery, materials science, financial modeling, logistics, cybersecurity, and defense. In 2025, the company achieved 99.99% two-qubit gate fidelity, setting a world record in quantum computing performance .
Headquartered in College Park, Maryland, IonQ has operations across North America, Latin America, EMEA, and APAC. Our quantum computing services have been available through all major cloud providers since 2021, while we also meet the needs of networking and sensing customers across land, sea, air, and space. IonQ is making quantum platforms more accessible and impactful than ever before. Learn more at IonQ.com .

articles.title_orig: Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
articles.title_zh: Rise in poverty is ‘a wake-up call for the world’, UN development chief says
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
The number of people living in “multidimensional” poverty has risen for the first time in 15 years, reaching 1.2 billion, as families struggle to meet their basic needs.
The finding comes in the 2026 update of the global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) published by the United Nations Development Programme ( UNDP ) and Oxford University, which measures overlapping hardship across health, education and standard of living.
The 1.2 billion figure represents 51.5 million more people than in the 2025 update .  Of this number, more than half are children – 617 million – and 83 per cent live in rural areas.
“The rise in poverty should be a wake-up call for the world,” said UNDP Administrator Alexander De Croo.
“Behind these figures are 1.2 billion people facing hardships that reinforce one another: hunger, missed schooling and a lack of clean water or electricity. This is unacceptable.”
The index was developed in 2010 to measure poverty beyond what people earn.
It examines 10 indicators of health, education and standard of living, such as nutrition and child mortality, years of schooling, and access to electricity, drinking water and sanitation.
A person is considered “multidimensionally poor” if they are deprived in one-third or more of the indicators.
Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia account for the overwhelming majority of deprivations across every indicator.
The 2026 update – which covers 108 countries, representing some 78 per cent of the global population – reveals that the increase in poverty is partly due to population growth outpacing efforts to improve living standards.
In 95 countries where no new survey data was available, updated population estimates increased the number of people counted as poor by nearly 16 million.
The remainder of the increase comes from 13 countries where data was gathered, reflecting the genuine change in poverty incidence and the associated demographic change, as well as differences in indicator coverage.
The updated surveys also revealed a mixed picture on the ground. Five of these countries – Egypt, Nepal, Tajikistan, Angola and Zambia – have reduced the share of people living in multidimensional poverty, however population growth outpaced poverty reduction in both Angola and Zambia, meaning that the total number of people living in poverty still increased.
Meanwhile, Nigeria provides an example of how fragile progress in tackling poverty can be. Although the country made significant reductions in multidimensional poverty in the 2010s, both the poverty rate and the number of people struggling to make ends meet have increased.
The international community has pledged to reduce the proportion of people living in poverty by at least half before the end of this decade, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
The authors of the 2026 MPI update believe that this target is achievable.
“We know progress is possible,” Mr. De Croo insisted. “Countries that have tackled these challenges together, rather than in isolation, have shown what determined action can achieve.”
UNDP reported that 33 countries have halved their MPI value in fewer than 15 years, including six in sub-Saharan Africa. In Eswatini, the share of people living in multidimensional poverty has fallen from nearly 39 per cent to eight per cent.
Meanwhile, China recorded the fastest reduction among countries with available data by halving its MPI value from 9.5 per cent to 4.2 per cent in just four years (2010-2014).
The shows that many countries continue to make progress, with some reducing poverty rapidly and at scale, underscoring both the urgency of renewed action and the possibility of success, the agency said.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Russian-Diesel Move Draws Pushback, Skepticism
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Russian-Diesel Move Draws Pushback, Skepticism
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism .
Trump, in a Truth Social post , accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union.
"The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote.
While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy.
"I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.
Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months.
The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin , ends the war against Ukraine.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.
Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal.
"While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.
Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent , however.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

articles.title_orig: IT'S BACK. THAT'S BIG. The All-Electric smart #2 Makes Its World Premiere at the Paris Motor Show
articles.title_zh: IT'S BACK. THAT'S BIG. The All-Electric smart #2 Makes Its World Premiere at the Paris Motor Show
articles.content_orig:
HANGZHOU, China , Oct. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- smart today celebrated the World Premiere of the all-new smart #2 at the Paris Motor Show, marking the return of its iconic two-seater for a new electric era.
Thirty years ago, the smart vehicle was presented as an art object beneath the Louvre Pyramid. Today, smart returns to Paris with the fully realised production smart #2.
Mr. Tong Xiangbei, Global CEO of smart, said: "The smart #2 is more than the return of a familiar silhouette; it is a demonstration of what our teams can achieve in the most demanding urban segment. Its World Premiere in Paris, followed by launches in Europe and China, opens an important new chapter for our global product family."
Mr. Kang Yi, Global CMO of smart, said: "The smart #2 expresses our core D.N.A. in a very pure way: Designed with Love, No Compromise on Safety, and Amazing Drives. It is small in footprint, but big in personality."
An Icon for a New Generation
Styled by the Mercedes-Benz Global Design Team, the smart #2 translates the character of smart's iconic two-seater into a contemporary new form, guided by its design philosophy of Love, Pure, Unexpected.
Clean proportions, short overhangs and its signature wheels-at-the-corners stance preserve the pure smart silhouette and maximise space. Unexpected details, including logo-inspired lighting and a contemporary interpretation of the iconic floating roof, reinterpret familiar smart cues.
Inside, bench-style seating and S-shaped cockpit make efficient use of the compact cabin, while carefully considered colours, materials and distinctive details bring warmth and individuality.
The Split Tailgate features an upper glass that opens independently in tight spaces, and a lower section that folds down as a loading platform or a 120-kg capacity seat.
smart #2 Couture Edition: Function becomes Fashion
As a surprise highlight, smart also unveiled the exclusive smart #2 Couture Edition, carrying the established "Function becomes Fashion" theme from concept to production.
Limited to 999 units in Europe and 999 units in China, the Couture Edition combines an Atelier White Matte exterior finish with a contrasting Platinum Gold roof, distinctive gold detailing and exclusive 16-inch Lyra rims. A numbered interior badge further underlines its limited-edition character.
Purpose-Built for Urban Mobility
Underpinning the smart #2 is the newly developed Electric Compact Architecture (ECA) platform, engineered specifically for smart's ultra-compact all-electric two-seater.
Measuring 2,746 mm in length, the smart #2 maximises usable space within its ultra-compact footprint. The ECA platform brings together intelligent packaging, a floor-mounted high-voltage battery, rear-wheel drive and advanced chassis technology.
Power comes from a rear-mounted 60 kW electric motor delivering 130 Nm of torque to the rear wheels.
For Europe, the smart #2 features a 35.8 kWh LFP battery, with a target combined WLTP range of 290 km. Supporting 65 kW DC fast charging, the smart #2 can charge from 10% to 80% state of charge within 20 minutes, while AC charging at up to 11 kW supports convenient everyday charging.
A curb-to-curb turning circle of just 6.95 metres makes navigating tight city streets and narrow parking spaces effortless.
The smart #2 features a five-link rear suspension, a first in its class, supporting confident and composed driving both in cities and on highways.
Central to the smart #2, the Tridion Cell Evo creates a robust protective structure around the passenger cabin without compromising the vehicle's compact dimensions. The vehicle also comes equipped with driver-assistance technologies including smart Pilot Assist and Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) with Stop & Go and Highway Assist.
The smart #2 Begins Its Global Market Rollout
Following its World Premiere in Paris, early ordering for the smart #2 will begin in Europe and China, bringing smart's iconic two-seater to two of the brand's key markets.
For Europe, the smart #2 will initially be offered in three core trim lines — Pure, Pure+ and Premium — alongside the limited Couture Edition.
For China, the smart #2 will be unveiled in Premium and Couture Edition variants.
Market-specific line-ups, pricing, specifications, equipment and availability will be communicated locally.

articles.title_orig: Sen. Marshall pays bakery bill after complaint goes viral
articles.title_zh: Sen. Marshall pays bakery bill after complaint goes viral
articles.content_orig:
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall settled his debts this weekend with a bakery in Kansas after a bill for hundreds of treats his campaign ordered for a 2020 event sat unpaid for six years.
Holly Thomas, the owner of the shop that made cookies, brownies and cupcakes for Marshall’s primary election watch party, said in a social media post on Friday that she will not vote for the senator in this year’s election, where he is facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, after he failed to pay the $678.75 he owed her small business.
“This isn’t about political parties or policy disagreements. It’s about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments,” Thomas said. “That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote.”
Thomas said she reached out several times but never heard back, noting that the lack of payment came as her business was just beginning and at the height of the coronavirus pandemic. “Six years later, I haven’t forgotten,” she said.
Marshall posted a screenshot of a payment for $1,300 on Saturday, showing that he had paid the half-a-decade-old cookie bill, and then some.
“We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double,” Marshall said on social media.
Thomas confirmed a few hours later that she can “finally mark the invoice paid.”
​The Republican senator is facing a competitive reelection race this fall, with voters’ strong disapproval of President Donald Trump and widespread economic anxiety raising the possibility that Kansas could send a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in nearly a century. A recent poll by The New York Times and Siena University showed Marshall tied with Hamilton at 45% among likely voters.
The repayment of the bakery bill come as Marshall, a former obstetrician-gynecologist, has faced criticism over a report last month that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical debt.
The New York Times found that he had filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills and at least 81 of those individuals were arrested for missing court dates. Democrats have leaned on the story in ads, accusing Marshall of disregarding people’s concerns about healthcare costs.
A spokesperson for Marshall told the Times that the longtime doctor spent many years treating patients regardless of their ability to pay.
“Judges issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, not doctors,” spokesperson Payton Fuller said in a statement to the outlet.
